notes.overview: Good communication is a clinical skill with a structure, not a personality trait. This topic covers the Calgary–Cambridge consultation structure, how listening and empathy change what patients tell you, how to check understanding, the SPIKES approach to breaking bad news, and what the GMC expects of you.
objectives: Describe the five stages of the Calgary–Cambridge guide and the two threads that run through them.
Distinguish the clinician's disease perspective from the patient's illness perspective (ideas, concerns, expectations).
Distinguish empathy from sympathy and compassion, and give an example of an empathic response.
Apply the six steps of SPIKES to a breaking-bad-news scenario.
Explain why health literacy and numeracy limit how patients use information and how to adapt your explanation.

sections.body:
Patient-centred communication organises the consultation around the patient’s concerns as well as the clinician’s need to reach a diagnosis. The Calgary–Cambridge guide gives a consultation five stages: initiating the session (preparation, rapport, finding out why the patient has come), gathering information, physical examination, explanation and planning, and closing. Two threads run through every stage: providing structure (signposting, summarising, logical order) and building the relationship (rapport, non-verbal communication, involving the patient).

When gathering information, separate the disease perspective (onset, character, associated symptoms, history) from the illness perspective: the patient’s ideas about what is wrong (“I think it is my heart”), their concerns (“my father died of this”), their expectations of the visit and the effect on daily life. Students often shorten this to ideas, concerns and expectations. If the illness perspective is never explored, a medically correct plan can still fail because the patient’s real worry was never addressed.

sections.h: Listening skills and why they work
sections.body:
Specific skills make the structure work.
- Open-to-closed cone: start with open questions (“tell me about the pain”), then narrow with closed questions to clarify; avoid leading and multiple questions.
- Active listening: let the patient finish, use silence, encourage with short prompts and check your understanding.
- Signposting and summarising: say what comes next, and summarise periodically so the patient can correct you.
- Non-verbal communication: eye contact, seating at the same level, not typing throughout.
- Empathy means noticing an emotion, naming it and acknowledging it (“that sounds frightening”). Sympathy expresses pity from a distance. Compassion adds a wish and an action to ease suffering.

Patients who feel heard tend to tell you more and to raise the real agenda early, which makes the later explanation easier to take in.

SPIKES is a six-step framework for delivering serious news, described for cancer care by Baile and colleagues in 2000 and used for any serious news. It is a map, not a script.
- Setting up: private space, seated, phones silenced; ask who the patient would like present.
- Perception: ask what they already understand or suspect.
- Invitation: ask how much they want to know, and whether now or later.
- Knowledge: give a warning shot (“I’m afraid the news is not what we hoped”), then plain words in small chunks, pausing to check understanding. Avoid jargon and euphemisms.
- Emotions: allow silence and respond with empathy before giving more information.
- Strategy and summary: agree next steps, summarise, answer questions, avoid pressing for decisions, and give a named contact.

You cannot assume that an explanation has landed. Check by asking the patient to say in their own words what they will tell their family, or what they will do next. Do this as a check on your explanation, not as a test of the patient.

Health literacy is the ability to find, understand and use health information. A Public Health England briefing (September 2015) reported a study in which 42% of working-age adults in England (aged 16 to 65) could not understand and make use of everyday health information, rising to 61% when the information also required numeracy skills. Treat this as a 2015 figure and check for newer data. The practical lessons are timeless: use plain words, give the most important message first, chunk information, avoid relying on percentages alone, and offer written or visual support. A fluent patient can still struggle when frightened or unwell.

The GMC’s Good medical practice, in effect from 30 January 2024, makes communication a professional duty rather than an optional skill. It requires doctors to treat patients with kindness, courtesy and respect, to communicate sensitively, to listen, to acknowledge concerns and to be alert to distress. It also requires doctors to be honest and open with patients, including when things go wrong, and not to let personal views affect patients’ care. Patients are expected to be partners in decisions about their care.

For students, these standards apply in miniature from the first day: introduce yourself and your role honestly, ask the patient’s permission before examining or taking a history, and never imply that you are more qualified than you are. Always read the current text on the GMC website, because the guidance is updated from time to time.

Ms Rahman, 47, attends alone for a breast biopsy result. The consultant uses a private room, sits down and silences the bleep (Setting). She asks what Ms Rahman understood the biopsy was for (Perception) and whether she wants the results today (Invitation). After a warning shot, she says plainly that the biopsy shows cancer, then stops (Knowledge). When Ms Rahman weeps, the consultant says, “This is a huge shock,” and waits (Emotions). Later she outlines the next steps in two or three stages, summarises, and gives the specialist nurse’s number (Strategy and summary).

- Students often think SPIKES is only for cancer. In fact it was first described in cancer care but suits any serious news.
- Students often think “I understand how you feel” is empathic. In fact it claims knowledge you cannot have; acknowledge what you observe instead.
- Students often think silence means the consultation is failing. In fact silence gives the patient time to take in news, and filling it with information is a common error.
- Students often think more information at once is more thorough. In fact people retain less when overloaded; chunk and check.

notes.h: Ethical reasoning, valid consent and Montgomery
notes.overview: Consent turns a clinician’s proposal into a lawful, ethical decision made with the patient. This topic covers the four principles of biomedical ethics, the elements of valid consent, what Montgomery changed about disclosing risk, and how GMC guidance expects shared decision making to work in practice.
objectives: Apply the four principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice) to a clinical dilemma and explain how they can conflict.
State the elements of valid consent and explain why consent is a process rather than a signature.
Explain the Montgomery test of material risk, including reasonable alternatives and the role of dialogue.
Explain the limits of the therapeutic exception.
Explain why a competent adult may refuse treatment even when the refusal seems unwise.

sections.h: The four principles and ethical reasoning
sections.body:
The most widely taught framework in medical ethics uses four prima facie principles, set out by Beauchamp and Childress and summarised for British readers by Gillon in 1994.
- Respect for autonomy: the patient’s right to make decisions about their own care, which depends on information and capacity.
- Beneficence: acting to benefit the patient.
- Non-maleficence: avoiding harm, which in practice means weighing harms against benefits.
- Justice: fairness in the distribution of care and in how people are treated.

“Prima facie” means each principle binds unless it conflicts with another. The framework does not give an answer; it gives a structure for reasoning. Typical conflicts are autonomy against beneficence (a capacitous patient refuses treatment you believe would help) and justice against beneficence (a treatment would help this patient but uses resources others need). A sensible approach is to identify the issue, gather the facts, name the principles in tension, apply the relevant law and professional guidance, reach a decision you can justify, and reflect afterwards. Ethics asks what you ought to do; law sets the minimum you must do, and the two are not identical.

Consent is valid when it is given by a person with capacity to decide, who has enough information to make that decision, and who gives it voluntarily. Each element can fail: capacity can be lost through delirium or intoxication, information can be too sparse or too technical, and voluntariness can be undermined by pressure from relatives or an implied threat that care will be withdrawn.

Consent is a process, not an event. It can be spoken, written or implied by actions (offering an arm for a blood test) and can be withdrawn at any time. A signed form is evidence that a discussion took place, not the consent itself. Good medical practice (2024) requires doctors to assume adults have capacity, involve patients in decisions, and obtain consent or other valid authority before examining or treating.

A capacitous adult may refuse any treatment, including life-saving treatment, for any reason or none. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 1).

Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 (decided 11 March 2015) is the leading case on what patients must be told. Mrs Montgomery, who was diabetic, had a baby with severe disabilities after a difficult delivery; her obstetrician had not told her of the risk of shoulder dystocia (about 9–10% for diabetic mothers in vaginal delivery). The Supreme Court held that the doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of material risks of the proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives.
- A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that this patient would.
- There is no fixed percentage below which a risk need not be mentioned: a small risk to fine hand movement may matter to a violinist and not to others.
- Reasonable alternatives must be explained too, and the court said advising requires dialogue with the patient, not a list of risks. GMC guidance adds the option of taking no action.
- The therapeutic exception, withholding information because disclosure would be seriously detrimental to the patient’s health, is limited and must not be abused. That a patient might decline is not a reason to withhold a risk.
The test moved from what a responsible body of doctors would say to what the patient needs to know.

sections.h: GMC guidance on decision making and consent

sections.body: Ms Hughes, 38, has type 1 diabetes, is of small stature and is carrying a baby expected to be large. Her obstetrician asks what matters most to her, explains vaginal birth and caesarean with their risks in plain numbers (for example “about 1 in 20”, which is 5%), invites questions and records the discussion. She does not withhold the risk of shoulder dystocia because she fears Ms Hughes will choose differently from her.

- Students often think a signed form means consent is valid. In fact the form is only evidence; consent needs capacity, understanding and voluntariness.
- Students often think risks below a certain percentage need not be mentioned. In fact Montgomery sets no threshold.
- Students often think a doctor may hold back a risk because the patient will probably refuse. In fact the therapeutic exception is narrow and concerns serious harm from the disclosure itself.
- Students often think an unwise refusal proves incapacity. In fact the law protects the right to make unwise decisions.

Typical conflicts are autonomy against beneficence (a capacitous patient refuses treatment you believe would help) and justice against beneficence (a treatment would help this patient but uses resources others need). A sensible approach is to identify the issue, gather the facts, name the principles in tension, apply the relevant law and professional guidance, reach a decision you can justify, and reflect afterwards. Ethics asks what you ought to do; law sets the minimum you must do, and the two are not identical.

What makes consent valid
Consent is valid when it is given by a person with capacity to decide, who has enough information to make that decision, and who gives it voluntarily. Each element can fail: capacity can be lost through delirium or intoxication, information can be too sparse or too technical, and voluntariness can be undermined by pressure from relatives or an implied threat that care will be withdrawn.

Consent is a process, not an event. It can be spoken, written or implied by actions (offering an arm for a blood test) and can be withdrawn at any time. A signed form is evidence that a discussion took place, not the consent itself. Good medical practice (2024) requires doctors to assume adults have capacity, involve patients in decisions, and obtain consent or other valid authority before examining or treating.

A capacitous adult may refuse any treatment, including life-saving treatment, for any reason or none. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 1).

Montgomery and material risk
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 (decided 11 March 2015) is the leading case on what patients must be told. Mrs Montgomery, who was diabetic, had a baby with severe disabilities after a difficult delivery; her obstetrician had not told her of the risk of shoulder dystocia (about 9–10% for diabetic mothers in vaginal delivery). The Supreme Court held that the doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of material risks of the proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives.
- A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that this patient would.
- There is no fixed percentage below which a risk need not be mentioned: a small risk to fine hand movement may matter to a violinist and not to others.
- Reasonable alternatives must be explained too, and the court said advising requires dialogue with the patient, not a list of risks. GMC guidance adds the option of taking no action.
- The therapeutic exception, withholding information because disclosure would be seriously detrimental to the patient’s health, is limited and must not be abused. That a patient might decline is not a reason to withhold a risk.
The test moved from what a responsible body of doctors would say to what the patient needs to know.

GMC guidance on decision making and consent
The GMC’s Decision making and consent guidance, in effect since 9 November 2020, reflects Montgomery and is built on shared decision making: the clinician brings knowledge of the options and the patient brings their values and priorities. It is summarised in seven principles, among them that all patients have the right to be involved in decisions, that decision making is an ongoing process built on meaningful dialogue, and that adults are presumed to have capacity. Practical expectations include:
- find out what matters to the patient so the information is relevant;
- explain the options and reasonable alternatives, including taking no action, with benefits, risks and burdens, in understandable terms;
- take a proportionate approach: a minor intervention needs a shorter discussion than major surgery;
- involve the wider team, give time, and make clear the patient can ask questions, change their mind or say no;
- record the discussion, including a choice not to hear some information.

Ms Hughes, 38, has type 1 diabetes, is of small stature and is carrying a baby expected to be large. notes.h: Mental capacity, best interests and consent by young people
notes.overview: Adults are presumed able to decide for themselves. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 sets out when that presumption is displaced and how decisions are then made in the person’s best interests. Young people are treated differently: 16- and 17-year-olds can consent as adults, and younger children can consent if Gillick competent.
objectives: State the five principles in section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
Apply the two-stage test in sections 2 and 3 and explain why capacity is decision-specific and time-specific.
Describe the steps of a best-interests decision under section 4.
Distinguish Gillick competence from the Fraser guidelines and state who can consent at 16 and 17.

sections.h: The principles and the test of capacity
sections.body:
Section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA), which applies in England and Wales, sets five principles: a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; they are not to be treated as unable to decide unless all practicable steps to help them have failed; they are not to be treated as unable to decide merely because they make an unwise decision; anything done for a person who lacks capacity must be in their best interests; and before acting, consider whether the purpose can be achieved in a less restrictive way.

Section 2 says a person lacks capacity for a matter if, at the material time, they are unable to make a decision for themselves because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain. This may be permanent or temporary. Age, appearance, or behaviour that might prompt assumptions cannot by themselves establish lack of capacity. Disputes are decided on the balance of probabilities. Most powers under the Act are not available for children under 16.

Assessment has two stages.
1. Diagnostic: is there an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain (for example dementia, delirium, intoxication, psychosis)?
2. Functional (section 3): because of that, is the person unable to understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it as part of making the decision, or communicate the decision by any means?

The “because of” link matters: a diagnosis does not by itself mean lack of capacity. The Supreme Court (A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52) said the first question is whether the person is unable to make the decision, and the second is whether that inability is because of the impairment. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, so it may fluctuate. Relevant information includes the foreseeable consequences of deciding one way, the other way, or not deciding. Retaining information only briefly does not rule out capacity, and a person is not unable to understand if they can grasp an explanation given in a suitable way, such as simple language or pictures. Before concluding that capacity is lacking, take practicable steps: choose the time and place, treat reversible causes such as pain, infection or poor hearing, and involve people who can help communication.

sections.h: Consent by children and young people
sections.body:
- Aged 16 or 17: section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 makes their consent to surgical, medical or dental treatment as effective as an adult’s. The MCA also applies from 16.
- Under 16: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority ([1986] AC 112, House of Lords, 1985) established that a child with sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed can give valid consent. Gillick competence is decision-specific.
- Fraser guidelines are the five criteria Lord Fraser set out for contraceptive advice or treatment without parental knowledge: attempts to involve parents have failed or the young person will not allow it; the young person understands the advice; they are very likely to have sex with or without contraception; their health is likely to suffer without it; and it is in their best interests. The NSPCC notes that, after a 2006 ruling (Axon), the guidelines can also be applied to advice and treatment for sexually transmitted infections and termination of pregnancy.
The law is more complex when a young person refuses treatment: those with parental responsibility, or a court, may in some circumstances authorise it. Seek senior and legal advice. Scotland has different rules.

A 14-year-old girl attends a sexual health clinic alone and asks for contraception. The clinician explores her understanding of the options and risks and why she does not want to involve her parents, encourages her to consider telling a trusted adult, and checks the Fraser criteria. If they are met, the clinician can provide contraception, as she is Gillick competent for this decision. The clinician also asks about her partner’s age and considers whether safeguarding action is needed, following local procedures and seeking senior advice.

- Students often think a 16-year-old must be Gillick competent. In fact from 16 the Family Law Reform Act 1969 and the MCA apply.

notes.overview: Confidentiality is what allows patients to tell you the truth, but it is not absolute. This topic covers the GMC’s principles for handling patient information, the three routes to lawful disclosure, how to respond to relatives who ask for information, and how students protect confidentiality.
objectives: Explain why confidentiality matters for individual care and for public trust.
List the three routes to lawful disclosure of identifiable information: consent, legal requirement and public interest.
Apply the GMC principle on sharing information for direct care, including when a patient objects.
Describe how to respond to a request for information from relatives or carers.
Explain how students and doctors protect confidentiality, including on social media.

sections.body:
Identifiable information can be shared in three main ways.
1. With the patient’s consent. For direct care, the GMC expects relevant information to be shared within the team providing care, because patients expect this and care would be unsafe without it, unless the patient has objected. For other purposes, such as teaching, research or non-clinical use (local clinical audit aside), explicit consent is the starting point.
2. Where the law requires it. Examples include a court order or a statutory duty to report. You should disclose only what the law requires.
3. Where it is justified in the public interest. Here the benefit to an individual or society from disclosure outweighs both the patient’s interest in confidentiality and the public interest in keeping health care confidential, for example to protect others from serious harm.

For a public-interest disclosure you balance the harm that may follow from disclosure against the harm from keeping the information confidential. You disclose only the minimum necessary to the appropriate person or body, consider whether you can ask for consent or tell the patient first, record your reasoning, and take advice if you are unsure. Disclosure in the public interest is discretionary and judgment-based, whereas a legal requirement is mandatory.

sections.h: Relatives, carers and sharing within teams
sections.body:
Relatives and carers are often the people patients most want involved, but being next of kin gives no automatic right to information. The usual approach is to ask the patient what they are happy for you to share and with whom, and to record it. You can always listen to what a relative tells you, because receiving information does not breach confidence; it is giving information that needs justification.

If a patient lacks capacity, the position follows the Mental Capacity Act 2005: information is shared where it is in the patient’s best interests, for example to establish their wishes or to plan care. If a patient has capacity and objects to sharing for their direct care, discuss the consequences, for example that withholding information from other professionals involved may limit the care they can provide, and respect the decision unless an exception applies.

Within teams, share what is relevant to the care that team member is providing, not the whole record. When sharing is unexpected, tell the patient, or check they know.

Practical steps follow from the principle that information must be protected from improper access, disclosure or loss.
- Do not discuss identifiable patients in lifts, corridors, canteens or on public transport.
- Anonymise case material for teaching and portfolios; do not copy identifiable records.
- Use approved systems, not personal devices or messaging apps, unless local policy permits.
- Good medical practice (2024) requires public communications, including social media, to be accurate and honest, and notes that messages in private groups may become public. Never post anything that could identify a patient.
- If unsure, ask your supervisor, the information governance lead or Caldicott guardian, or your defence body. If you breach confidentiality, report it promptly and follow local procedures, which may include telling the patient.

notes.h: Mental health: common conditions, epidemiology and assessment
notes.overview: Mental health problems are common, shaped by social circumstances and closely linked to physical health. This topic uses the 2023/4 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey to size the problem, introduces the biopsychosocial view, describes core features of common conditions, and covers assessment, including the mental state examination and NICE advice on risk scales.
objectives: Describe the main findings of the 2023/4 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey with their year labels, and explain what a prevalence survey can and cannot show.
Explain the biopsychosocial and stress–vulnerability views of mental disorder and give examples of social influences.
Describe the core features of depression, anxiety disorders, psychosis and self-harm.
List the components of a mental state examination and give an example of each.
Explain NICE NG225’s advice on risk assessment tools and risk stratification after self-harm.

sections.h: How common are mental health conditions?
sections.body:
In the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (APMS), common mental health conditions (also called common mental disorders) are depression and anxiety disorders, identified with the Clinical Interview Schedule–Revised (CIS-R), a structured interview about symptoms in the past week. The 2023/4 survey was run by NatCen with the University of Leicester and City St George’s for NHS England, with fieldwork from March 2023 to July 2024. These are figures for England; check for newer data.
- 22.6% of 16–64-year-olds had a condition in 2023/4, versus 18.9% in 2014 and 17.6% in 2007: up 3.7 percentage points since 2014 and 5.0 since 2007.
- Women 27.8% versus men 17.3% (aged 16–64); 25.8% of 16–24-year-olds.
- 26.2% in the most deprived fifth of areas versus 16% in the least deprived: about 1.6 times.
- 32.9% of people with a limiting physical health condition versus 12.6% without: about 2.6 times.
- Lifetime non-suicidal self-harm (aged 16–74): 10.3%, up from 3.8% in 2007 (about 2.7 times).
- 47.7% of people with symptoms reported receiving treatment, up from 39.4% in 2014.
A prevalence survey counts people with a condition; it cannot show why numbers changed, and the reasons (real increases, greater willingness to report) are debated.

No single cause explains mental disorder. The biopsychosocial view treats biological factors (genetic vulnerability, physical illness, substance use), psychological factors (thinking patterns, early experiences, coping) and social factors (poverty, housing, isolation, discrimination, violence, work) as interacting. The stress–vulnerability model adds that illness develops when stress exceeds a person’s capacity to cope, so the same stressor affects people differently.

The 2023/4 survey shows social patterning: the higher rate in the most deprived fifth of areas and among 16–24-year-olds. Causation runs both ways, since poverty raises risk and illness can reduce income and connection. Mental and physical health also interact: long-term conditions bring pain, disability and financial strain, and depression can make a physical condition harder to manage. Stigma and poor access delay help-seeking, so the treatment figure of 47.7% leaves many without help.

- Depression: persistent low mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, and reduced energy are core features; others include disturbed sleep, appetite change, poor concentration, guilt, aches and hopelessness. Severe depression may include suicidal thoughts.
- Anxiety disorders: excessive, hard-to-control worry (generalised anxiety), sudden surges of fear with physical symptoms (panic) and avoidance.
- Psychosis: hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus), delusions (fixed false beliefs) and disorganised thinking, often with reduced insight.
- Self-harm: deliberate self-injury or self-poisoning, often a way of coping with distress. It does not always involve intent to die but needs assessment each time, including what it does for the person and what support they need.
- Suicidal thoughts range from passing wishes to specific plans; ask directly, calmly and without judgement.

sections.h: Assessment and the mental state examination
NICE guidance on self-harm and depression
sections.body:
NICE guideline NG225, Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (published 7 September 2022; last reviewed 16 August 2024), sets out psychosocial assessment after self-harm: why it occurred, the person’s needs, strengths, vulnerabilities and protective factors, leading to a care and safety plan; mental health professionals should include a risk formulation in every psychosocial assessment (recommendation 1.6.6).
Recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.4 say not to use risk assessment tools and scales, or global stratification into low, medium or high risk, to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should be offered treatment or discharged. Care should rest on needs and safety, not a score or label.
For depression, NICE guideline NG222 (published 29 June 2022) covers treatment and management in adults, matching first-line treatment to severity, with a matched-care approach. Psychological therapies and medication are both options, depending on severity, history and preference. Check current guidance before applying it.

Aisha, 19, a first-year student, describes six weeks of low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest and a feeling that others would be “better off” without her. The doctor notes slow speech and a flat, tearful affect while Aisha says she is “fine”, asks directly about suicidal thoughts and plans, and finds thoughts of not wanting to live but no plans. She uses no score or label: she explores supports and protective factors, agrees a safety plan, considers physical causes such as thyroid disease, discusses treatment options and arranges early follow-up.

- Students often think mental health conditions are uncommon. In fact 22.6% of 16–64-year-olds in England had a common mental health condition in 2023/4.
- Students often think a risk score or low/medium/high label predicts who will harm themselves. In fact NICE NG225 advises against using them to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment.
- Students often think depression is just sadness. In fact it is a pattern of persistent symptoms that impairs function.
- Students often think self-harm always means a suicide attempt. In fact reasons vary, though each episode needs assessment.
- Students often think mental and physical health are separate. In fact 32.9% of people with a limiting physical condition had a common mental health condition, versus 12.6% without.

- Self-harm: deliberate self-injury or self-poisoning, often a way of coping with distress. It does not always involve intent to die but needs assessment each time, including what it does for the person and what support they need.

Assessment combines history, observation and physical investigation where relevant: presenting problem and course, past psychiatric and medical history, medication, alcohol and drugs, family and social circumstances, risk, and a collateral history with the patient’s agreement where possible.

- mood (the patient’s report) and affect (the emotion you observe, and whether it fits what they say);
- thought: form (flow, coherence), content (delusions, obsessions, suicidal or violent thoughts) and possession (thoughts inserted, withdrawn or broadcast);

notes.h: The Mental Health Act 1983 and the 2025 reforms
notes.overview: The Mental Health Act 1983 allows people to be detained and treated for mental disorder without their consent when strict criteria and safeguards are met. sections.h: Purpose and relationship to the Mental Capacity Act
sections.body:
The Mental Health Act 1983 (MHA), which applies in England and Wales, lets people be detained in hospital for assessment or treatment of mental disorder when necessary. Being “sectioned” means being detained under a particular section. Most mental health care is voluntary.

The MHA is separate from the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA). It depends on mental disorder and risk, not capacity: a person with capacity can be detained and treated for their mental disorder without consent, and lack of capacity alone does not justify detention under it. The Act authorises treatment of the mental disorder only; treatment of unrelated physical illness needs consent, or MCA authority if the person lacks capacity. Care should be the least restrictive that is safe. The treatment powers in Part 4 do not apply to people held only under the short-term powers (section 4 before the second recommendation, 5(2), 5(4), 135 or 136), so they keep the same right to consent or refuse as informal patients (section 56).

Section 2 (assessment): mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment (or assessment then treatment), and detention is needed for the person’s own health or safety or to protect others. Two medical recommendations (one from a specially approved doctor) and an application, usually by an approved mental health professional (AMHP). Up to 28 days; not renewable.
Section 3 (treatment): mental disorder making hospital treatment appropriate, treatment necessary for health or safety or to protect others and not possible without detention, and appropriate treatment available; same recommendations and application; up to 6 months initially, renewable.
Section 4 (emergency): in urgent necessity, when waiting for section 2 would involve undesirable delay; one medical recommendation; lapses after 72 hours unless a second recommendation arrives, when detention continues under section 2.
Section 5(2): the doctor or approved clinician in charge of an inpatient’s treatment (or their nominee) can hold a voluntary inpatient for up to 72 hours while assessment is arranged. Section 5(4): a mental health or learning disability nurse’s power, up to 6 hours, for an inpatient being treated for mental disorder when a doctor is not immediately available.
Sections 135 and 136: a magistrate’s warrant lets police enter premises (135); police may remove a person who appears mentally disordered and in immediate need of care or control, from anywhere except a home, to a place of safety for up to 24 hours, extendable by 12 hours (136).
Section 17A: a community treatment order after section 3, with recall possible.

- Appeal: a detained person can apply to the Mental Health Tribunal, which is independent and decides whether discharge is appropriate, or ask the hospital managers to review detention. At present the window to apply under section 2 is 14 days from admission.
- Independent mental health advocate (IMHA): a statutory advocate who helps patients understand and use their rights. Legal representation at the tribunal is available through legal aid.
- Second opinion: three months after medication for mental disorder was first given in the period of detention, it can continue only if a capable patient’s consent is certified or a second opinion appointed doctor (SOAD) certifies that it is appropriate (section 58). For ECT (section 58A), outside an emergency, a capable patient’s refusal cannot be overridden, and a patient who lacks capacity needs a SOAD certificate and must not have a valid advance refusal.
- Nearest relative: a relative fixed by a statutory list (section 26), whose powers include objecting to a section 3 application and ordering discharge, which the responsible clinician can bar on grounds of dangerousness (section 25). The 2025 Act plans to replace the role with a patient-chosen nominated person.

notes.h: Patient safety, incidents and the duty of candour
notes.overview: Most patient harm comes from weaknesses in systems, not just from individual mistakes. This topic covers the system approach and the Swiss cheese model, how NHS England expects incidents to be recorded and learned from, and the difference between the statutory and professional duties of candour.
objectives: Distinguish the person approach from the system approach, and active failures from latent conditions.
Use the Swiss cheese model to explain how an incident arises.
Describe the purpose of the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework and the Learn from patient safety events service.
Distinguish the statutory duty of candour (regulation 20) from the professional duty of candour.
Describe what to do, as a student or doctor, when something goes wrong.

sections.body:
A patient safety incident is an unintended or unexpected event in health care that did or could have harmed a patient. James Reason (BMJ, 2000) contrasted two approaches.
- The person approach focuses on individuals’ unsafe acts, such as forgetfulness or carelessness, and responds with blame, retraining or discipline.
- The system approach assumes humans are fallible and asks how and why the defences failed: we cannot change the human condition, but we can change the conditions under which people work.
Active failures are the unsafe acts (slips, lapses, mistakes, violations) of people in direct contact with patients. Latent conditions are hidden weaknesses created by designers, procedure writers and managers, such as time pressure, understaffing or unclear handover; they can lie dormant for years.
In the Swiss cheese model each layer of defence is a slice with holes that open, close and move. One hole usually does no harm; harm occurs when holes in several layers line up. Most incidents involve both active failures and latent conditions, so fixing the system prevents repeats better than blaming the last person.

sections.h: How the NHS in England responds to incidents
sections.body:
The Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF) is NHS England’s approach to responding to patient safety incidents, aimed at learning and improvement. It replaced the Serious Incident Framework, is a contractual requirement under the NHS Standard Contract, and organisations had to move to it within 12 months of its publication (by autumn 2023). Its four key aims are: compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; and supportive oversight.
Learn from patient safety events (LFPSE) is the national NHS system for recording and analysing patient safety events. It replaced the National Reporting and Learning System, decommissioned on 30 June 2024. Events are recorded whether or not they cause harm, because near misses show where defences are weak. Check NHS England for the current position.

There are two duties, which overlap but differ.
The statutory duty (regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, enforced by the Care Quality Commission) falls on registered providers. It applies after a notifiable safety incident: an unintended or unexpected incident during a regulated activity that, in a health care professional’s reasonable opinion, could result in or appears to have resulted in a listed outcome. For health service bodies these include death, severe harm, moderate harm and prolonged psychological harm. Moderate harm means harm needing a moderate increase in treatment (for example an unplanned return to surgery or extra time in hospital) that is significant but not permanent. The provider must notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, with a true account of the facts known, advice on further enquiries and an apology (an expression of sorrow or regret), then follow up in writing and keep records.
The professional duty (joint GMC and NMC guidance) applies to individual doctors and nurses whenever care causes, or could cause, harm or distress: tell the person (or advocate, carer or family where appropriate), apologise, offer an appropriate remedy or support if possible, and explain the short- and long-term effects.

A good review asks what happened, how and why, not who to blame. It builds a timeline, identifies where defences failed, and looks for contributory factors in the task, the individual, the team and communication, the environment and equipment, and the organisation (staffing, policies, culture). It asks what barrier could have caught the problem, for example a system that routes test results to a named person with a deadline for acknowledgement.
Involving the patient and family is part of the process, as is supporting staff. Outputs should be actions that change the system, not advice to “be more careful”.

sections.h: What to do when something goes wrong
sections.body:
The first priority is the patient: make them safe and get senior help. Then:
- Be open and honest. Good medical practice (2024) requires doctors to be open and honest with patients if things go wrong, put matters right if possible, apologise and explain the effects.
- Record the facts in the notes, without speculation or altering earlier entries.
- Report the incident through the local system.
- Cooperate with reviews, support colleagues, and raise concerns if patients are at risk.
As a student, tell your supervisor promptly about any error or near miss. Do not fix it quietly, conceal it, or explain it to the patient yourself; the clinical team leads the conversation with the patient, and you may be asked to give a factual account of what you saw.

A 63-year-old man had a chest X-ray whose report recommended a follow-up CT, but no process assigned the result to a named clinician and it was never actioned. Blaming the last doctor would miss the latent conditions: no tracking of recommendations, unclear ownership, and a high volume of results. The professional duty of candour requires that he is told, offered an apology and explanation, and supported. The organisation considers the statutory threshold, records the event in LFPSE, and focuses learning on a safer follow-up system.

- Students often think incidents are caused by the last person to touch the patient. In fact there are usually latent conditions behind the active failure.

- Students often think only harmful incidents need recording. In fact LFPSE records events whether or not they cause harm.
- Students often think the statutory and professional duties are the same. In fact the statutory duty rests on organisations with defined harm thresholds; the professional duty rests on individuals and applies whenever care causes or could cause harm or distress.

notes.h: Professionalism: Good medical practice, equality law and speaking up
notes.overview: Professionalism is the set of values and behaviours that justify public trust. This topic uses Good medical practice 2024 as the framework, covers honesty, fairness and speaking up, and explains the Equality Act 2010, including the duty to make reasonable adjustments, as it applies to patients and colleagues.
objectives: Name the four domains of Good medical practice 2024 and give a duty from each.
Explain why honesty, integrity and fair treatment are central to professional trust.
Distinguish direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation under the Equality Act 2010.
Describe the duty to make reasonable adjustments and give examples.
Describe appropriate ways to raise a concern about a colleague or a system.

sections.body:
Several duties sit under the heading of trust.
- Honesty and integrity: your conduct should justify public trust. Be honest about your experience, qualifications and role, in financial dealings and in research, and in all communications.
- Fairness: treat patients fairly and do not let personal views affect their care. Do not refuse or delay treatment because of a patient’s contribution to their condition. Do not abuse, discriminate against, bully or harass anyone on the basis of personal characteristics.
- Boundaries and conflicts of interest: declare conflicts and do not exploit patients’ vulnerability or limited medical knowledge.
- Public communication: anything you say publicly, including on social media, must be accurate and honest, and messages in private groups may become public. Follow the GMC’s detailed guidance on social media.
- Candour: be open and honest with patients if things go wrong.

These duties apply from the start of training. For students, honesty includes being truthful about your role when meeting patients, accurate in attendance and coursework, and open about your own mistakes and concerns.

The Equality Act 2010 applies in Great Britain and protects against discrimination because of a protected characteristic (section 4): age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Socio-economic disadvantage is not one of them, a common error.
- Direct discrimination (section 13): less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic.
- Indirect discrimination (section 19): a provision, criterion or practice applying to everyone that puts people with a characteristic at a particular disadvantage and cannot be shown to be a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
- Discrimination arising from disability (section 15).
- Harassment (section 26): unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment.
- Victimisation (section 27): subjecting someone to a detriment because they did a protected act, such as bringing a claim, giving evidence or making a complaint under the Act.
Services, including health services, must not discriminate (section 29). Disabled people are also entitled to reasonable adjustments (section 20): where a rule, practice, physical feature or lack of an auxiliary aid puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage, providers must take reasonable steps to avoid it, and the duty is anticipatory. Public authorities, including NHS organisations, have the public sector equality duty (section 149).

GMP expects doctors to contribute to a culture in which concerns can be raised safely. If you see behaviour or a system that puts patients at risk, or that is discriminatory, you should raise it.
- Raise concerns about behaviour through your workplace’s policy.
- If resources or systems put patients at risk, protect patients first, then raise the issue with those able to act.
- Take advice before reporting a colleague who may be unfit to practise, for example from your supervisor, a senior colleague or a professional body.
- Leaders must make it possible to raise concerns safely, and nobody must obstruct someone raising a concern.
- Keep a factual, contemporaneous record of what you saw.

As a student, raise concerns with your supervisor, personal tutor or the medical school’s named contact, and keep patient information confidential when you do. Medical schools have fitness to practise procedures for students, and honesty and a willingness to take feedback usually count heavily in how concerns are viewed.

Mr Obi, 29, has a learning disability and needs a blood test; he has left clinics before because the waiting room was loud and staff spoke quickly. The practice makes adjustments in advance: a longer appointment at a quiet time, an easy-read leaflet, a chance to meet the phlebotomist beforehand, and his support worker if he wants her there. - Students often think social class or low income is protected. In fact the nine section 4 characteristics do not include it.

- Students often think a doctor may delay care for a patient who “caused” their illness. In fact GMP says not to refuse or delay treatment because of this.
- Students often think raising a concern is disloyal. In fact it is a core professional duty.

- Discrimination arising from disability (section 15).
- Harassment (section 26): unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment.
- Victimisation (section 27): subjecting someone to a detriment because they did a protected act, such as bringing a claim, giving evidence or making a complaint under the Act.
Services, including health services, must not discriminate (section 29). Disabled people are also entitled to reasonable adjustments (section 20): where a rule, practice, physical feature or lack of an auxiliary aid puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage, providers must take reasonable steps to avoid it, and the duty is anticipatory. Public authorities, including NHS organisations, have the public sector equality duty (section 149).

Speaking up
GMP expects doctors to contribute to a culture in which concerns can be raised safely. If you see behaviour or a system that puts patients at risk, or that is discriminatory, you should raise it.
- Raise concerns about behaviour through your workplace’s policy.
- If resources or systems put patients at risk, protect patients first, then raise the issue with those able to act.
- Take advice before reporting a colleague who may be unfit to practise, for example from your supervisor, a senior colleague or a professional body.
- Leaders must make it possible to raise concerns safely, and nobody must obstruct someone raising a concern.
- Keep a factual, contemporaneous record of what you saw.

As a student, raise concerns with your supervisor, personal tutor or the medical school’s named contact, and keep patient information confidential when you do. Medical schools have fitness to practise procedures for students, and honesty and a willingness to take feedback usually count heavily in how concerns are viewed.

Clinical application
Mr Obi, 29, has a learning disability and needs a blood test; he has left clinics before because the waiting room was loud and staff spoke quickly. The practice makes adjustments in advance: a longer appointment at a quiet time, an easy-read leaflet, a chance to meet the phlebotomist beforehand, and his support worker if he wants her there. The phlebotomist explains each step in plain words and asks for his consent. Treating him exactly as everyone else would have disadvantaged him; capacity is assessed for this decision and he is supported to decide.

Common misconceptions
- Students often think treating everyone the same is always fair. In fact identical treatment can disadvantage some groups, which underlies indirect discrimination and reasonable adjustments.
- Students often think social class or low income is protected. In fact the nine section 4 characteristics do not include it.
- Students often think professionalism only matters in front of patients. In fact GMP covers conduct in public life, including social media.
- Students often think a doctor may delay care for a patient who “caused” their illness. In fact GMP says not to refuse or delay treatment because of this.
- Students often think raising a concern is disloyal. In fact it is a core professional duty.

notes.overview: Health depends heavily on the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age. This topic covers the social gradient, the Dahlgren–Whitehead model, the Marmot Review (2010) and its 2020 update with their key numbers, and practical ways clinicians can respond to patients’ circumstances.
objectives: Define the social determinants of health and describe the Dahlgren–Whitehead model.
Explain the social gradient and the idea of proportionate universalism.
State the six policy objectives of the 2010 Marmot Review.
Describe the main findings of the 2020 update (Marmot 10 Years On) with their year labels.
Describe practical ways clinicians can respond to the social circumstances of patients.

sections.body:
Social determinants of health are the non-medical conditions that shape health: the circumstances in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, and the wider forces, such as income, housing, education, employment and power, that shape those circumstances.
The Dahlgren and Whitehead (1991) model shows layers of influence on health. At the centre are fixed factors (age, sex, genes). Around them are personal lifestyle, then the physical and social environment, and finally wider socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions. Outer layers constrain what is possible for inner ones: choices about diet or smoking are made within limits of income, housing, work and community, so interventions aimed only at behaviour often have limited effect.
The Marmot Review states the social gradient plainly: health follows a gradient, and everyone below the top has a greater risk of worse health than those at the top. It affects the whole population, not only the poorest.

Several overlapping pathways link social position to health.
- Material: low income and insecurity limit access to food, warm dry housing, transport and safe work.
- Psychosocial: chronic stress, low control, insecurity and discrimination affect mental and physical health.
- Behavioural: smoking, diet, alcohol and activity vary with price, availability, culture and stress.
- Access and quality of care: cost, transport, digital exclusion, time off work or lower health literacy make services harder to use.
- Life course: early disadvantage accumulates; the 2010 Marmot Review gave the best start in life for every child the highest priority.
Numbers link these pathways to outcomes. In the 2023/4 mental health survey, 26.2% of people in the most deprived fifth of areas had a common mental health condition, against 16% in the least deprived fifth. The 2010 review reported that people in the poorest neighbourhoods die on average seven years earlier than those in the richest.

Fair Society, Healthy Lives (the Marmot Review, 2010) proposed six objectives: give every child the best start in life (the highest priority); enable all children, young people and adults to maximise their capabilities and have control over their lives; create fair employment and good work for all; ensure a healthy standard of living for all; create and develop healthy and sustainable places and communities; and strengthen the role and impact of ill health prevention.
It argued for proportionate universalism: universal action to reduce the steepness of the gradient, with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. Targeting only the most deprived would miss the gradient; a uniform approach would leave the greatest need unmet.
Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020) found that life expectancy gains had slowed and that health inequalities had widened; press coverage reported that life expectancy had stopped rising for the first time in over 100 years. It concluded that public spending cuts were likely to have harmed health and widened inequalities, and that population health depends on living conditions, not just on the health service.

Inequalities are measured by comparing outcomes (life expectancy at birth, healthy life expectancy, mortality, disease prevalence) across groups defined by area deprivation (for example the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods against the least), region, ethnicity and other characteristics. Period life expectancy is a snapshot from current death rates.
The 2020 review reported, for England:
- Life expectancy at birth rose from 78.7 to 79.6 years for men (a gain of 0.9) and from 82.6 to 83.2 years for women (a gain of 0.6) between 2010 and 2018, against gains of 2.2 years (men) and 1.5 years (women) in 2000 to 2008.
- Female life expectancy fell in the most deprived 10% of neighbourhoods between 2010–12 and 2016–18.
- In 2016–18 men in the North East could expect 77.9 years against 80.7 in London, and women 81.7 against 84.5: a gap of 2.8 years for both.
The slowdown was greatest in more deprived areas.

Clinicians cannot fix social conditions alone, but they can respond.
- Ask sensitively about work, money, housing, caring and isolation when they affect the problem in front of you.
- Adapt communication to health literacy: a 2015 PHE briefing reported that 42% of working-age adults in England could not understand and use everyday health information, rising to 61% when numeracy was needed. Use plain language and check understanding; do not assume a missed appointment means a patient does not care.
- Reduce barriers with flexible appointments, phone or in-person options and interpreters. This is proportionate universalism in practice: all patients are served, with extra effort where barriers are greatest.
- Refer and signpost to welfare rights, housing, employment or debt advice.
- Advocate, and work with public health, local government and the voluntary sector, using local data to see who is not being reached.

Mr Khan, 52, has COPD and lives in a damp rented flat. He misses weekday morning clinics because he is a zero-hours delivery driver, and rations heating because of cost. A purely medical review would repeat inhaler advice. A fuller response asks about housing, income and work, offers a different appointment time and phone follow-up, refers him to welfare and housing advice (with a supporting letter for repairs), and asks the practice to look for other patients missing appointments for similar reasons.

- Students often think health inequalities concern only the very poorest. In fact the gradient runs through the whole population.
- Students often think poor health is mainly lifestyle choice. In fact choices are made within conditions set by income, housing and work.
- Students often think life expectancy has risen steadily for decades. In fact the 2020 review found improvements slowed after 2010 and female life expectancy fell in the most deprived tenth.
- Students often think proportionate universalism means targeting only the most deprived. In fact it is universal provision with greater intensity for greater disadvantage.

cards.f: What are the five stages of the Calgary–Cambridge guide?
cards.b: Initiating the session; gathering information; physical examination; explanation and planning; closing the session. Providing structure and building the relationship run through all of them.
cards.ex: The five stages follow the order of a consultation; two threads (structure and relationship) apply to every stage.

cards.f: Disease perspective vs illness perspective
cards.b: Disease perspective: the clinician’s biomedical questions (onset, character, history). Illness perspective: the patient’s ideas, concerns, expectations and the effect on their life.
cards.ex: Both are needed: the disease perspective gets the diagnosis, the illness perspective gets the patient’s real agenda.

cards.f: Why start with open questions and then narrow to closed ones?
cards.b: Open questions let the patient set out their story and raise issues you would not think to ask about; closed questions then clarify detail. Starting closed can cut off key information.
cards.ex: Open questions widen what you hear; closed questions then refine it, so the order matters.

cards.f: How does a brief summary during the history help the consultation?
cards.b: It shows the patient they have been heard, lets them correct errors or add detail, and signals a move to the next part, so it supports both structure and the relationship.
cards.ex: Summarising does two jobs: it checks accuracy and it builds trust.

cards.f: What do the letters of SPIKES stand for?
cards.b: Setting up, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary.
cards.ex: The sequence moves from preparation, through finding out what they know and want to know, to the news, the reaction and the plan.

cards.f: After you give a diagnosis the patient goes silent and stares at the floor. What should you do first?
cards.b: Pause and allow the silence, then acknowledge the emotion (“this is a lot to take in”) before offering more information or treatment options.
cards.ex: In SPIKES, emotions are handled before strategy: people cannot process a plan while overwhelmed.

cards.f: In the Perception step a patient says, “My sister had the same lump and it was cancer.” What does this tell you?
cards.b: She already suspects cancer and has a personal frame of reference, so a warning shot can be brief, and you should explore what her sister’s experience means to her.
cards.ex: Perception tells you where to begin and which fears or beliefs you need to address.

cards.f: Empathy vs compassion
cards.b: Empathy: recognising and acknowledging another person’s feelings. Compassion: empathy plus a wish to relieve the suffering and action to do so.
cards.ex: Compassion adds motivation and action to empathic understanding.

cards.f: Why might a patient with low health literacy misunderstand a correct explanation?
cards.b: Because jargon, abstract percentages or long explanations exceed what they can process. A 2015 PHE briefing reported 42% of working-age adults in England struggled with everyday health information.
cards.ex: Literacy and numeracy are separate barriers to understanding, so check and adapt rather than assume.

cards.f: Name the four principles of biomedical ethics.
cards.b: Respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.
cards.ex: They are prima facie principles: each binds unless it conflicts with another.

cards.f: Why do autonomy and beneficence sometimes conflict?
cards.b: A capacitous patient may refuse a treatment the clinician believes would benefit them. Autonomy supports respecting the refusal; beneficence pulls towards treating. In law, the capacitous refusal prevails.
cards.ex: The conflict arises because patients’ values may differ from clinicians’ view of benefit; the law gives priority to a capacitous adult’s choice.

cards.f: Montgomery test vs the older “responsible body of doctors” approach to disclosing risk
cards.b: Older approach: what a responsible body of doctors would tell. Montgomery: what a reasonable person in the patient’s position, or this patient, would attach significance to.
cards.ex: Montgomery shifts the test from the profession’s practice to the patient’s needs.

cards.f: A risk occurs in 1 in 1000 cases (0.1%). Must it be mentioned?
cards.b: There is no fixed cut-off. It must be mentioned if it would be significant to a reasonable person in this patient’s position or to this patient, for example a small risk to hand function in a violinist.
cards.ex: Materiality depends on the patient and the consequences, not only on the percentage.

cards.f: What is the therapeutic exception and how limited is it?
cards.b: Disclosure may be withheld only where it would be seriously detrimental to the patient’s health. It is limited, must not be abused, and is not satisfied just because the patient might refuse.
cards.ex: It protects patients from serious harm caused by the information itself, not clinicians from refusals.

cards.f: A patient signed a consent form but cannot say what the operation involves. Is the consent valid?
cards.b: Not safely. The form is evidence, not consent. Check capacity and understanding, repeat the discussion and record it before proceeding.
cards.ex: Valid consent requires understanding; a signature alone does not supply it.

cards.f: Why must reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, be discussed?
cards.b: Montgomery requires the patient to be aware of reasonable alternatives, and GMC guidance includes the option of taking no action, so that they can weigh the options; without them, the choice is not genuinely informed.
cards.ex: You cannot choose between options you do not know about.

cards.f: A patient says, “I do not want to hear the risks; just do what you think is best.” What should you do?
cards.b: You can respect this choice, but make sure they know information is available on request, offer essential information, and record the discussion.
cards.ex: Patients may choose not to be told; respecting that is consistent with autonomy if recorded.

cards.f: Informed vs voluntary consent
cards.b: Informed: the patient has enough information to understand the decision. Voluntary: the decision is the patient’s own, free of pressure or coercion. Both are required, along with capacity.
cards.ex: Valid consent can fail on information, voluntariness or capacity independently.

cards.f: State the five principles in section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
cards.b: Presume capacity; take all practicable steps to help before concluding incapacity; unwise decisions are not incapacity; act in best interests; choose the less restrictive option.
cards.ex: Principles 1 to 3 protect autonomy; principles 4 and 5 govern decisions once capacity is lacking.

cards.f: What four abilities does section 3 test?
cards.b: To understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it as part of the decision, and communicate the decision. Inability in any one means inability to decide.
cards.ex: These are the functional elements of the test; the diagnostic element is the impairment of mind or brain.

cards.f: Why is capacity described as decision-specific and time-specific?
cards.b: Ability can vary with the complexity of the decision and fluctuate with illness (for example delirium), so a person may be able to decide one thing now but not another, or the same thing later.
cards.ex: Capacity is not a label for a person but an assessment of one decision at one time.

cards.f: A patient with moderate dementia refuses a flu vaccination, saying she dislikes injections. What should you consider?
cards.b: Presume capacity for this decision and assess it, helping her understand the information. If she can understand, retain, weigh and communicate, her refusal stands.
cards.ex: A diagnosis does not remove capacity, and the decision is hers if she meets the section 3 test.

cards.f: A man chooses to refuse dialysis, and the team thinks this is unwise. Does this show he lacks capacity?
cards.b: No. An unwise decision does not by itself show lack of capacity (section 1). Assess whether he can understand, retain, weigh and communicate.
cards.ex: Section 1 protects the right to make decisions others disagree with.

cards.f: Gillick competence vs Fraser guidelines
cards.b: Gillick competence: a child with sufficient understanding and intelligence can consent to a decision. Fraser guidelines: five criteria for giving contraceptive advice or treatment to a young person without parental knowledge.
cards.ex: Gillick is the general principle; Fraser is the application to contraception (later extended to wider sexual health).

cards.f: A 17-year-old consents to a routine procedure and her parents object. Whose consent counts?
cards.b: Hers. Under section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969, consent of a 16- or 17-year-old to treatment is as effective as an adult’s (with capacity presumed).
cards.ex: At 16 and 17 consent follows the adult rules; Gillick competence is for younger children.

cards.f: Why can relatives not simply consent for an adult who lacks capacity?
cards.b: Under the MCA the clinician makes a best-interests decision after consulting them. Relatives consent only if they hold a valid lasting power of attorney or deputyship that covers the decision.
cards.ex: The Act gives authority to decide through best interests or formal legal appointments, not through family relationship.

cards.f: What must you consider when making a best-interests decision?
cards.b: All relevant circumstances including the chance of regaining capacity; the person’s participation, past and present wishes, beliefs and values; the views of those consulted; and no motive of bringing about death in life-sustaining decisions.
cards.ex: Section 4 forms a checklist that centres the person, not the clinician’s preference.

cards.f: What are the three routes to lawful disclosure of identifiable patient information?
cards.b: With the patient’s consent; where the law requires it; or where it is justified in the public interest.
cards.ex: The GMC principle names explicit consent, with exceptions for legal requirement and public interest.

cards.f: Why does the GMC allow relevant information to be shared for direct care without asking each time?
cards.b: Patients expect those caring for them to know what they need to know, and safe care often depends on it. The expectation is that the patient has not objected.
cards.ex: Reasonable expectations and safety support sharing within the team, but patients’ objections are respected.

cards.f: Disclosure required by law vs disclosure in the public interest
cards.b: Required by law: mandatory (for example a court order). Public interest: discretionary, based on weighing harm from disclosure against harm from silence.
cards.ex: The first is a duty; the second is a justified decision you must be able to explain.

cards.f: A man phones the ward asking about his wife’s test results. What should you do?
cards.b: Do not disclose. Say you cannot discuss patients without their permission, listen if he wants to share concerns, and ask the patient whether she is happy for him to be told.
cards.ex: Next of kin has no automatic right to information; the patient decides if capacitous.

cards.f: What should you consider before a public-interest disclosure?
cards.b: Weigh harm to the patient and to trust in confidential services against the benefit of disclosure, disclose only the minimum necessary to the appropriate person, and record your reasoning.
cards.ex: Proportionality and minimum disclosure are the safeguards.

cards.f: A capacitous patient says, “Please do not tell my GP.” What is the correct approach?
cards.b: Discuss the consequences of not sharing, such as implications for continuing care. If the objection remains, respect it unless the law requires disclosure or it is justified in the public interest.
cards.ex: Direct-care sharing is conditional on the patient not having objected.

cards.f: Does the duty of confidentiality end when a patient dies?
cards.b: No. Good medical practice 2024 says to treat information about patients as confidential, including after death.
cards.ex: Trust in confidentiality would be weakened if patients thought it ended at death.

cards.f: Two students discuss a named patient on the bus. What is the problem?
cards.b: Information may be overheard by people who should not hear it, which is improper disclosure. Discuss patients only in appropriate places, and anonymise where possible.
cards.ex: Protecting information from improper disclosure includes casual conversation in public places.

cards.f: Anonymised vs identifiable information
cards.b: Anonymised information cannot identify the patient and can generally be used without consent; identifiable information can, and so needs a lawful basis. Combinations of details can make an apparently anonymous case identifiable.
cards.ex: The GMC advises using the least information needed and anonymised information where practicable.

cards.f: What proportion of 16–64-year-olds in England had a common mental health condition in the 2023/4 APMS?
cards.b: 22.6%, compared with 18.9% in 2014 and 17.6% in 2007. These are survey estimates for England and should be checked against newer data.
cards.ex: Always quote the year: the 2014 and 2007 figures are lower.

cards.f: In APMS 2023/4, 26.2% of people in the most deprived fifth of areas and 16% in the least deprived fifth had a common mental health condition. What does this show?
cards.b: An association between area deprivation and mental health (about 1.6 times higher), consistent with a social gradient. A survey like this cannot by itself show cause and effect.
cards.ex: The ratio shows a gradient, but the direction of causation needs other evidence.

cards.f: Why are people with long-term physical conditions more likely to have common mental health conditions?
cards.b: Pain, disability, uncertainty, isolation and financial strain raise the risk of depression and anxiety, and depression can in turn worsen self-management of the physical condition.
cards.ex: The relationship runs in both directions, which is why holistic assessment matters.

cards.f: What does the stress–vulnerability model propose?
cards.b: Illness develops when stress exceeds a person’s capacity to cope, which depends on their biological, psychological and social vulnerability. The same stress affects people differently.
cards.ex: It explains why not everyone exposed to the same stress becomes ill.

cards.f: Mood vs affect in the mental state examination
cards.b: Mood: the patient’s own account of their sustained inner state. Affect: the emotion the examiner observes, including range and appropriateness to what is being said.
cards.ex: A patient may say their mood is “fine” while the observed affect is flat or tearful.

cards.f: A patient says “I’m fine” but is tearful, speaks slowly and avoids eye contact. What does this suggest?
cards.b: A mismatch between reported mood and observed affect and behaviour. It suggests possible depression and the need to explore further, including thoughts of self-harm.
cards.ex: Observation provides information the patient may not volunteer.

cards.f: Hallucination vs delusion
cards.b: Hallucination: a perception without an external stimulus (for example hearing voices). Delusion: a fixed, false belief held despite evidence to the contrary.
cards.ex: One is a disturbance of perception, the other of belief.

cards.f: A 19-year-old with six weeks of low mood says others would be “better off without me”. What is the appropriate next step?
cards.b: Ask directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent, and assess needs and protective factors. Agree a safety plan, involve senior help and arrange early follow-up.
cards.ex: Direct, non-judgemental exploration is the start of a psychosocial risk formulation.

cards.f: What does NICE NG225 say about risk scales after self-harm?
cards.b: Do not use risk assessment tools and scales, or low/medium/high risk stratification, to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged (recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.4).
cards.ex: Care should follow a psychosocial assessment of needs and safety, not a score.

cards.f: How long can a patient be detained under section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983?
cards.b: Up to 28 days from admission; it cannot be renewed.
cards.ex: If longer detention is needed, section 3 is used.

cards.f: How long does section 3 last initially?
cards.b: Up to 6 months, then it can be renewed.
cards.ex: Section 3 is for treatment when the diagnosis and needs are established.

cards.f: Section 2 vs section 3
cards.b: Section 2: assessment, up to 28 days, not renewable. Section 3: treatment, up to 6 months initially, renewable. Both need two medical recommendations and an application, usually by an AMHP.
cards.ex: Match the section to whether the aim is assessment or treatment.

cards.f: Section 5(2) vs section 5(4)
cards.b: Both hold a voluntary inpatient. 5(2) is a doctor’s power for up to 72 hours. 5(4) is a nurse’s power for up to 6 hours, used when a doctor is not immediately available.
cards.ex: The nurse’s power is a bridge to a doctor’s assessment.

cards.f: Why is capacity not the test for detention under the MHA?
cards.b: The Act depends on mental disorder and the need for assessment or treatment for health or safety or protection of others. A person with capacity can be detained, and lack of capacity alone does not justify detention.
cards.ex: Capacity is assessed under the MCA; detention under the MHA turns on disorder and risk.

cards.f: A voluntary patient with a mental disorder wants to leave a general ward and is thought to be at risk. Which power may a doctor use?
cards.b: Section 5(2): a doctor’s holding power for up to 72 hours while assessment for section 2 or 3 is arranged.
cards.ex: Section 136 is a police power to remove someone to a place of safety; section 5(2) is the doctor’s power for inpatients.

cards.f: A detained patient with capacity refuses antipsychotic treatment. Can treatment for his mental disorder be given?
cards.b: Yes in principle if he is detained under a section to which the treatment rules apply, such as 2 or 3, with the Act’s safeguards, because the MHA does not depend on consent; the short-term holding powers give no power to treat. Physical treatment unrelated to the disorder still needs consent or MCA authority.
cards.ex: The MHA authorises treatment of the mental disorder only.

cards.f: Name three safeguards for a detained patient.
cards.b: Right of appeal to the Mental Health Tribunal or hospital managers; an independent mental health advocate; a second opinion (SOAD) certificate for medication beyond three months unless a capable patient’s consent is certified.
cards.ex: Safeguards balance the intrusion of compulsion.

cards.f: Why must you check the commencement status of the Mental Health Act 2025?
cards.b: It amends the 1983 Act in stages by regulations. At the time of writing (November 2026), you must check which provisions, such as the serious-harm test or nominated person, are in force.
cards.ex: Law can be enacted but not yet in force; using the wrong version could be unlawful.

cards.f: Person approach vs system approach to error
cards.b: Person approach: blames individuals’ unsafe acts and responds with blame or retraining. System approach: assumes people are fallible, asks why defences failed and changes working conditions.
cards.ex: Reason argued the system approach suits healthcare, because the same conditions produce repeat errors.

cards.f: Active failures vs latent conditions
cards.b: Active failures: unsafe acts by people in direct contact with patients, with immediate effect. Latent conditions: hidden weaknesses from decisions upstream (design, procedures, management) that can lie dormant for years.
cards.ex: Active failures are the visible end; latent conditions set the stage.

cards.f: Why does the Swiss cheese model say harm often needs several failures?
cards.b: Each layer of defence has holes that open and close. A hazard reaches the patient only when holes in several layers align, so a single failure is usually caught.
cards.ex: Multiple defences mean single failures are usually contained; alignment causes harm.

cards.f: What are the four key aims of PSIRF?
cards.b: Compassionate engagement and involvement; system-based approaches to learning; considered and proportionate responses; supportive oversight.
cards.ex: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework, moving towards learning and proportionate response.

cards.f: Why does LFPSE record events that cause no harm?
