cards.b: Near misses and no-harm events show where defences are weak before a patient is harmed, giving earlier and more frequent learning than harm alone.
cards.ex: Learning does not depend on harm having occurred.

cards.f: Statutory vs professional duty of candour
cards.b: Statutory (CQC regulation 20): on organisations, triggered by a notifiable safety incident with defined harm levels. Professional (GMC and NMC): on individuals, applies whenever care causes or could cause harm or distress.
cards.ex: Different bearers, different thresholds; both involve openness and apology.

cards.f: A patient has an unplanned return to theatre after surgery. Which statutory harm category might this indicate?
cards.b: Moderate harm, which includes harm needing a moderate increase in treatment such as an unplanned return to surgery and which is significant but not permanent.
cards.ex: Regulation 20 gives unplanned return to surgery as an example of a moderate increase in treatment.

cards.f: As a student you notice a patient has been given the wrong dressing, with no harm. What should you do?
cards.b: Tell your supervisor, who ensures the patient is safe, decides what the patient is told and records it. It should be reported even though no harm resulted.
cards.ex: No-harm events and near misses are still learning opportunities, and students should not conceal them.

cards.f: What should an apology under the duty of candour contain?
cards.b: An expression of sorrow or regret about the incident, given with a true account of the facts known, explanation of effects and the support offered, not a defensive account.
cards.ex: Regulation 20 defines an apology as an expression of sorrow or regret about the notifiable safety incident.

cards.f: Name the four domains of Good medical practice 2024.
cards.b: Knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; trust and professionalism.
cards.ex: It took effect on 30 January 2024.

cards.f: List the nine protected characteristics in the Equality Act 2010.
cards.b: Age; disability; gender reassignment; marriage and civil partnership; pregnancy and maternity; race; religion or belief; sex; sexual orientation.
cards.ex: Socio-economic status is not on the list.

cards.f: Direct vs indirect discrimination
cards.b: Direct (s13): less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic. Indirect (s19): a rule or practice that applies to all but disadvantages a protected group and is not justified.
cards.ex: Direct is about the reason for treatment; indirect is about the effect of a neutral rule.

cards.f: Harassment vs victimisation under the Equality Act
cards.b: Harassment (s26): unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment. Victimisation (s27): a detriment because someone did a protected act, such as bringing a claim, giving evidence or making a complaint under the Act.
cards.ex: Harassment concerns the conduct itself; victimisation is retaliation for a protected act such as complaining.

cards.f: Why is the duty to make reasonable adjustments called anticipatory?
cards.b: Providers must think ahead about barriers disabled people may face rather than waiting for individual requests, so adjustments are in place before they are needed.
cards.ex: Waiting for a request can itself disadvantage people who cannot ask.

cards.f: A practice only allows appointments to be booked by an online form. A patient with a learning disability cannot use it. What legal issues arise?
cards.b: The practice rule may put disabled people at a disadvantage (indirect discrimination) and engages the duty to make reasonable adjustments, for example by taking bookings by phone or in person.
cards.ex: A neutral rule can still disadvantage a group; adjustments remove the barrier.

cards.f: A patient has lung cancer and has smoked for decades. A colleague suggests delaying treatment because the illness is self-inflicted. What does GMP say?
cards.b: Do not refuse or delay treatment because of a patient’s contribution to their condition; treat patients fairly and do not let personal views affect care.
cards.ex: Fairness is a duty; moral judgements about causes do not justify delay.

cards.f: A student sees a colleague mock a patient’s accent. What is the appropriate response?
cards.b: Raise it promptly with a supervisor or tutor through the proper route, keeping a factual account, rather than ignoring it or confronting the colleague publicly.
cards.ex: GMP expects people to speak up about unfair behaviour, using workplace processes.

cards.f: Why must public posts on social media be accurate and honest even in private groups?
cards.b: Public communication must be accurate and honest, and messages in private groups can become public, so they can damage trust and may breach confidentiality.
cards.ex: Private is not guaranteed; the professional standard applies wherever you communicate.

cards.f: State the six policy objectives of the 2010 Marmot Review.
cards.b: Best start in life for every child; maximise capabilities and control; fair employment and good work; healthy standard of living for all; healthy and sustainable places and communities; strengthen ill health prevention.
cards.ex: Giving every child the best start in life was the highest priority.

cards.f: Social gradient vs a simple poor-versus-rich divide
cards.b: The gradient means health improves step by step with social position across the whole population. A simple divide would imply only the poorest have worse health.
cards.ex: Marmot: everyone below the top has a greater risk of worse health.

cards.f: Name four pathways linking social position to health.
cards.b: Material (income, housing), psychosocial (stress, control), behavioural (smoking, diet), and access to quality care; accumulation over the life course also matters.
cards.ex: The pathways interact; focusing on one alone misses much of the picture.

cards.f: Proportionate universalism vs targeting
cards.b: Proportionate universalism: services for everyone with scale and intensity proportionate to disadvantage. Targeting: only the most deprived, which misses the gradient.
cards.ex: It addresses the whole gradient while giving more to those with greater need.

cards.f: Life expectancy in England rose by 0.9 years for men and 0.6 for women between 2010 and 2018, compared with 2.2 and 1.5 in 2000–2008. What does this show?
cards.b: Gains slowed markedly after 2010 (Marmot 10 Years On, 2020), with the slowdown greatest in more deprived areas.
cards.ex: Comparing periods reveals a change in trend, not just a level.

cards.f: In 2016–18 men in the North East had a life expectancy of 77.9 years and London men 80.7. What is the gap?
cards.b: 2.8 years (the report gave the same gap for women: 81.7 versus 84.5).
cards.ex: Compute the difference: 80.7 − 77.9 = 2.8.

cards.f: Why do interventions aimed only at individual behaviour often have limited effect?
cards.b: Behaviour is shaped by income, housing, work and community, so people cannot always act on advice. The 2020 review rejected the idea that poor health simply reflects poor choices.
cards.ex: Dahlgren and Whitehead show behaviour sits within wider layers of influence.

cards.f: A patient repeatedly misses morning clinics because of shift work and cannot afford travel. What is a proportionate response?
cards.b: Offer a different appointment time or phone follow-up, address travel costs if possible, and ask about work and finances, rather than labelling him non-compliant.
cards.ex: Reducing barriers meets need where it is greatest.

cards.f: Describe the layers of the Dahlgren–Whitehead model (1991).
cards.b: From the centre outwards: fixed individual factors (age, sex, genes); lifestyle; physical and social environment; wider socio-economic, cultural and environmental conditions.
cards.ex: Outer layers constrain what is possible in inner layers.

questions.q: In the SPIKES framework, which step is the moment when the clinician asks how much information the patient wants to be given?
options: Perception
Invitation
Knowledge
Strategy and summary
questions.why: Invitation comes before Knowledge: you ask how much detail the patient wants (and who they want present) before you deliver the news. Perception, the preceding step, finds out what they already believe. Knowledge is delivery of the news. Strategy and summary closes the conversation with a plan.
optWhy: Perception is about finding out what the patient already understands or suspects. It is easy to confuse with invitation because both come before the news, but it is about their existing knowledge, not how much more they want.
Invitation is the step where you ask how much the patient wants to know and whether they want others present.
Knowledge is the step where the news itself is delivered, with a warning shot and plain language. It comes after you have found out how much they want to know.
Strategy and summary is the final step, covering the plan, summary and support. It is not where you decide how much information to give.
questions.clue: The question asks when the patient is asked how much they want to be told.
questions.concept: SPIKES steps and their purposes.

followUp.q: A patient says, “Just tell me the main point; I will ask my daughter for the details later.” Which step of SPIKES does this reply belong to?
options: Perception: it shows what the patient already knows
Emotions: it shows that the patient is upset
Setting up: it shows who should be in the room
Invitation: the patient is telling you how much detail they want
followUp.why: This reply tells you how much detail the patient wants, which is the purpose of the Invitation step. It does not reveal what they already understand (Perception), and it says nothing about their emotional reaction (Emotions) or the room arrangements (Setting up), although it may lead you to invite the daughter to a later visit.

questions.q: A 62-year-old man has just been told he has a serious lung condition. He says quietly, “I knew it would be something like this,” and looks at the floor. Which response best shows empathy?
options: “I know exactly how you feel.”
“Let me explain the staging system so you know what the results mean.”
“This is clearly very hard to hear. Would it help if we paused for a moment?”
“Don’t worry, we will get through this together,” followed straight away by treatment options
questions.why: The patient has reacted emotionally, so the priority is to acknowledge it and give him time. Naming the difficulty and offering a pause does both. Reassurance, claims to know his feelings and further information all skip past the emotion.
optWhy: It names and acknowledges the emotion and gives the patient control of the pace.
This is premature reassurance and moves to strategy before the emotion has been acknowledged, so the patient may feel unheard.
It claims an understanding you cannot have and makes the conversation about the clinician, which can shut the patient down.
It delivers more information while the patient is still reacting, which ignores the emotions step and is likely to be forgotten.
questions.clue: He looks at the floor and speaks quietly after the news: an emotional reaction to acknowledge.
questions.concept: Empathic responses acknowledge emotion before giving more information.

followUp.q: A mother is told her child needs to be admitted to hospital and says, “I should have brought her in earlier.” Which reply is most empathic?
options: “There is nothing for you to feel guilty about, so please do not think about it.”
“We will now go through the admission paperwork.”
“It sounds as though you are being very hard on yourself; you brought her in and that is what matters.”
“Most parents say that, and it is usually untrue.”
followUp.why: Naming her guilt and gently reframing it acknowledges the feeling without dismissing it. Telling her to stop thinking about it dismisses the emotion, moving to paperwork ignores it, and generalising (“most parents say that”) minimises her individual worry.

questions.q: A patient with three months of headaches has told you the full symptom history and had a normal examination. You plan to reassure her, but she says, “I still think there is a tumour.” Which part of the consultation was most likely missed?
options: Exploring her ideas and concerns (the illness perspective)
Signposting
Moving from open to closed questions
A summary of the biomedical history
questions.why: A complete history and normal examination answer the disease perspective. Her belief about a tumour is a concern that should have been asked about, so that the reassurance could address it directly.
optWhy: Signposting tells the patient what will happen next. It is about structure, and a signposting failure would leave her confused about the process, not holding an unexplored fear.
The open-to-closed cone concerns how questions are asked. She gave a full history, so the questioning style did not hide the symptoms; what was missing was her view of what they meant.
A summary of the history would check accuracy of facts, but it would not by itself reveal what she feared the headaches meant.
Her fear of a tumour was a concern that should have been elicited and addressed before the explanation.
questions.clue: She holds a specific belief (a tumour) that was not addressed.
questions.concept: Ideas, concerns and expectations belong to the illness perspective.

followUp.q: A man attends repeatedly with back pain that investigations cannot explain. He finally says, “My brother was paralysed after a fall.” What does this show?
options: That his pain is probably psychological in origin
A previously unspoken concern that explains why he keeps returning and needs addressing
That the clinician should end the consultation sooner
That the history taking was too structured and should be abandoned
followUp.why: His fear of paralysis is an unexpressed concern. Addressing it explicitly is likely to reduce repeat attendance. It does not show the pain is psychological (the fear is a reason for worry, not a cause), and structure is not the problem. The remedy is to ask about ideas and concerns, not to shorten or abandon the consultation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old woman has attended for the results of a CT scan which shows a likely cancer. Using SPIKES, outline how you would conduct the conversation.
markScheme: Setting up: private space, seated, interruptions minimised, ask whether she wants someone with her
Perception: ask what she understands and suspects about the scan so far
Invitation: ask how much she wants to know and whether she wants it now
Knowledge: warning shot, plain language in small chunks, pause and check understanding
Emotions and strategy: respond empathically to her reaction (allow silence), then agree next steps, summarise and give a contact
questions.modelAnswer: I would begin by choosing a private room, seating us both at the same level, silencing my phone and asking whether she wanted anyone present (Setting up). I would ask what she understood about the scan and what she had been told or feared (Perception), then ask how much detail she wanted today (Invitation). I would give a warning shot such as “I’m afraid the scan shows something serious”, then give the result in plain, short sentences, pausing to check what she had taken in (Knowledge). I would expect strong emotion, allow silence and acknowledge her reaction before moving on (Emotions). Finally I would explain the next steps in a small number of clear stages, summarise, invite questions, avoid pressing her for decisions, and make sure she had a named contact and written information (Strategy and summary).
questions.concept: SPIKES gives a structured, patient-led approach to serious news.

questions.q: According to Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11, when is a risk “material”?
options: When a responsible body of medical opinion would regard it as worth mentioning
When it occurs in more than a fixed percentage of cases, such as 1 in 100
When a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the doctor knows or should know that this patient would
When the patient asks about it directly
questions.why: Montgomery defines a material risk by reference to the patient: what a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to consider significant, or what the doctor knows or should know this patient would consider significant. It rejects both the professional-practice test and any fixed percentage cut-off, and it is not limited to questions the patient asks.
optWhy: This is the older professional-practice approach to disclosure that Montgomery moved away from; it asks what doctors would say, not what the patient needs to know.
Montgomery sets no numerical threshold. A very small risk can be material if the consequence matters to this patient.
This is the Supreme Court’s test, which focuses on the patient rather than the profession.
The duty is to take reasonable care that the patient is aware of material risks; it is not limited to questions the patient thinks to ask.
questions.clue: The question asks for the legal definition of a material risk.
questions.concept: Montgomery test of material risk.

followUp.q: Which approach to disclosing a 0.5% risk of permanent hoarseness is consistent with Montgomery?
options: Discuss it with a professional singer, because it is likely to be significant to her, even though the risk is small
Omit it for everyone, because it is below 1%
Mention it only if the surgeon’s colleagues routinely do so
Mention it only if the patient asks about voice problems
followUp.why: A voice-related risk is likely to matter greatly to a singer, so it is material to her even though it is rare. There is no 1% cut-off, the test is not what the surgeon’s colleagues do, and the duty does not depend on the patient asking.

questions.q: A 45-year-old professional violinist is offered hand surgery. The surgeon believes the roughly 1 in 500 risk of nerve injury affecting fine finger movement is too small to mention. What is the best view of this decision under Montgomery?
options: The risk should be mentioned only if the violinist asks about it
The decision is correct, because risks below 1% need not be disclosed
The risk should be discussed, because it is likely to be significant to this patient’s livelihood
The decision is correct, provided other surgeons would also omit the risk
questions.why: Hand function is central to the violinist’s work, so a reasonable person in her position, and the doctor who knows her occupation, would see the risk as significant. The test is patient-focused and has no percentage threshold, and it does not depend on what colleagues do or on the patient asking.
optWhy: No such percentage rule exists. The rarity of a risk does not decide whether it is material.
The materiality test looks at this patient, and the consequence of nerve injury is of particular importance to a violinist.
Reliance on what colleagues would do is the older professional-practice test, which Montgomery replaced for risk disclosure.
The doctor must take reasonable care that the patient knows about material risks and does not rely on the patient asking.
questions.clue: A violinist, a risk to fine finger movement and a surgeon who omits it because it is rare.
questions.concept: Materiality depends on the patient’s circumstances.

followUp.q: A man who relies on his sense of smell for his work as a perfumer is offered nasal surgery with a 1 in 300 risk of permanent loss of smell. The surgeon thinks the risk is too small to matter. Which view is correct?
options: The surgeon is right because 1 in 300 is below the level that must be disclosed
The surgeon is right if a panel of nasal surgeons would not mention it
The surgeon should wait to see whether the patient raises the issue
The surgeon should discuss the risk, because it is likely to be significant to this patient
followUp.why: Loss of smell would affect the perfumer’s livelihood, so the risk is material to him. Montgomery has no numerical cut-off and does not use the practice of a surgical panel as the test, and the surgeon must volunteer the information rather than wait for questions.

questions.q: A man with capacity has signed a consent form for a hernia repair. Before the procedure he tells the nurse, “I have no idea what they are going to do; I just signed where I was told.” What is the correct course of action?
options: Proceed, because he can withdraw consent during the operation if he objects
Stop and arrange for a clinician to repeat the discussion, check his understanding and record it before proceeding
Proceed, because he has capacity and has signed
Proceed after his wife confirms she understands the operation
questions.why: The man has capacity but has not been given or has not taken in the information, so consent is not valid. The operation should not proceed until the discussion has been repeated and recorded. The signature, a relative’s understanding or the theoretical right to withdraw cannot replace his own informed agreement.
optWhy: Consent requires understanding as well as a signature, so it is not yet valid.
Capacity and a signature are not enough: consent also needs adequate information. The form is only evidence that a discussion took place.
A relative’s understanding does not substitute for the patient’s. A capacitous adult must give their own consent.
The right to withdraw does not cure a lack of understanding, and he could not exercise it once under anaesthesia.
questions.clue: He says he signed where he was told and has no idea what is planned.
questions.concept: Valid consent needs understanding, not just a signature.

followUp.q: A patient with capacity is given an information leaflet in a language she cannot read, signs the form and is taken to theatre. Which statement is correct?
options: Her consent is valid, because she signed the form
Her consent is valid, because the leaflet was given to her
Her consent may not be valid, because she has not understood the information
Her consent is valid if her husband can read the leaflet
followUp.why: Valid consent depends on the patient understanding the information. A signature or the handing over of a leaflet does not show understanding, and her husband’s reading does not replace her own understanding. An interpreter or other appropriate support is needed.

questions.q: Explain the Montgomery test of material risk and describe how it should change the way a doctor discusses risk with a patient.
markScheme: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11: doctor must take reasonable care that the patient is aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives
A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the doctor is or should be aware that this patient would
Replaces the professional-practice test; no fixed percentage threshold
Dialogue: find out what matters to the patient and tailor the discussion rather than reading a list
Therapeutic exception is limited; record the discussion
questions.modelAnswer: In Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 the Supreme Court held that a doctor must take reasonable care to ensure that a patient is aware of material risks of the proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient’s position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should be aware that the particular patient would. This replaced the earlier approach of asking what a responsible body of doctors would disclose, and it sets no percentage threshold. In practice a doctor should find out what matters to the patient, have a conversation rather than recite a list, explain alternatives including no treatment, and use understandable terms. The therapeutic exception, withholding information that would be seriously detrimental to the patient’s health, is limited and cannot be used merely because the patient might refuse. The doctor should record what was discussed.
questions.concept: Montgomery makes disclosure patient-centred and dialogue-based.

questions.q: Which statement correctly reflects the first principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
options: A person with a diagnosed mental disorder must be assumed to lack capacity until shown otherwise
A person who makes a decision that clinicians consider unwise lacks capacity for that decision
Capacity must be confirmed by two doctors before a person is allowed to refuse treatment
A person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it
questions.why: The first principle of the MCA is that capacity is presumed and the burden is on showing it is lacking. A diagnosis is not proof, an unwise decision is not proof, and the Act does not require two doctors to confirm capacity before a person can decide.
optWhy: This reverses the presumption and treats diagnosis as proof; the Act requires an assessment of the specific decision.
Section 1 states that a person is not to be treated as unable to decide merely because they make an unwise decision.
The Act contains no two-doctor requirement for presuming capacity; any decision-maker can assess capacity for a decision.
Section 1 presumes capacity and requires evidence of incapacity.
questions.clue: The question asks which statement correctly reflects the presumption of capacity.
questions.concept: The MCA presumes capacity.

followUp.q: A 70-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia declines a dental procedure. The team assume he lacks capacity because of his diagnosis. Which statement is correct?
options: His diagnosis establishes that he lacks capacity for all decisions
His capacity for this decision must be assumed unless the assessment shows he cannot decide because of his impairment
His refusal shows he lacks capacity because dental procedures are beneficial
His relatives can consent because he has a psychotic disorder
followUp.why: The Act presumes capacity and requires decision-specific assessment, so a diagnosis does not establish incapacity. A refusal that others find unwise is not evidence of incapacity, and relatives do not gain a general power to consent because of a diagnosis.

questions.q: A 78-year-old woman with a chest infection and delirium refuses intravenous treatment. She can repeat the explanation of her condition after ten minutes and says clearly that she does not want the treatment, because she believes the nurses are trying to poison her. Which section 3 ability is most clearly impaired?
options: Retaining the information
Using or weighing the information, because a delusional belief prevents her from balancing the options
Communicating the decision
Understanding the information
questions.why: The functional test looks at which of the four abilities fails. Understanding, retention and communication are intact because she can repeat the information and state her choice, but her belief about poisoning stops her weighing the information. The cause is a disturbance of brain function (delirium), which satisfies the diagnostic stage. Reversible causes should be treated and capacity reassessed.
optWhy: She can repeat the explanation, which suggests she understands it. Her difficulty lies in what she does with the information.
She recalls the explanation ten minutes later, so retention is intact. In any case, short retention would not by itself rule out capacity.
She cannot use the information in a rational decision because her belief overrides it.
She states her choice clearly, so communication is not the problem.
questions.clue: She can repeat the explanation, communicates clearly, but acts on a belief that nurses are poisoning her.
questions.concept: Using or weighing information is impaired by delusions.

followUp.q: A 25-year-old with severe anorexia nervosa says she understands that refusing food could kill her, but believes she is “not allowed to eat” and cannot weigh the consequence against the belief. Which section 3 ability is most clearly impaired?
options: Using or weighing the information as part of the decision
Understanding the information, because she cannot repeat it
Retaining the information, because she forgets it quickly
Communicating the decision, because she cannot express a choice
followUp.why: She can state the information and express a choice, so understanding, retention and communication are intact. The impairment is in using or weighing the information, as her belief prevents her from balancing the consequences. This matches the pattern in which the person can recite facts but cannot apply them to the decision.

questions.q: A 17-year-old girl with capacity consents to a routine minor operation. Her father says he does not agree and refuses to sign. What is the legal basis for proceeding?
options: Section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969: her consent is as effective as an adult’s
Parental consent is required until she reaches 18
A court order is needed whenever a parent objects
She must be assessed as Gillick competent and meet the Fraser criteria
questions.why: The Family Law Reform Act 1969, section 8, gives 16- and 17-year-olds the same power to consent to treatment as adults, and capacity is presumed under the MCA. Parental objection does not override it for this purpose, and neither Gillick competence nor the Fraser criteria are needed.
optWhy: Gillick competence is the route for children under 16, and the Fraser criteria apply to contraceptive advice and treatment. Neither is required for a 17-year-old.
At 16 and 17 a young person’s consent to treatment is as effective as if of full age.
This ignores section 8, which gives 16- and 17-year-olds the power to consent to their own treatment.
A court is not needed to act on valid consent from a young person who has the power to consent.
questions.clue: She is 17, has capacity, and her father objects.
questions.concept: At 16 and 17 young people consent like adults.

followUp.q: A 16-year-old with capacity agrees to a blood test and her mother objects. Which statement is correct?
options: Her mother’s consent is required because she is under 18
She must satisfy the five Fraser criteria first
A court must approve before the test can be done
Her consent is effective under the Family Law Reform Act 1969, section 8
followUp.why: Section 8 makes consent by a 16- or 17-year-old as effective as an adult’s. Parental consent is not required, the Fraser criteria relate to contraception rather than to general treatment, and no court approval is needed for valid consent.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl attends alone requesting contraception. Explain how Gillick competence and the Fraser guidelines apply.
markScheme: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA: child with sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed can consent
Competence is decision-specific; assess understanding of the options, risks and consequences
Fraser guidelines are five criteria for contraception without parental knowledge
Name at least three criteria (parents involved or will not be told; understands advice; likely to have sex anyway; health will suffer; best interests)
Does not remove safeguarding duties; seek senior advice where concerns
questions.modelAnswer: Under Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority ([1986] AC 112), a child who has sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand fully what is proposed can give valid consent, and competence is judged for each decision. I would assess whether she understands the options, benefits, risks and alternatives. The Fraser guidelines apply specifically to contraceptive advice and treatment without parental knowledge: I would be satisfied that she understands the advice, that attempts to involve her parents have failed or that she will not allow them to be told, that she is very likely to have sex with or without contraception, that her physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it, and that provision is in her best interests. If these are met, I can provide contraception without parental consent. I would also consider safeguarding concerns, such as her partner’s age, and seek senior advice where needed.
questions.concept: Gillick is the principle; Fraser guidelines apply it to contraception.

questions.q: Which situation is the clearest example of a disclosure that is required by law, rather than a discretionary public-interest disclosure?
options: A teacher asks for the patient’s diagnosis to plan classroom support
A court orders a hospital to hand over a patient’s records
A doctor decides to inform the authorities about a patient who refuses to do so and poses a risk of serious harm to others
A relative asks for information because she is the patient’s next of kin
questions.why: A court order is a legal requirement and the doctor must comply, disclosing only what is required. A decision to inform an authority about risk to others is weighed by the doctor and is justified by the public interest. Next of kin status and requests from third parties do not create a legal duty.
optWhy: A court order is a legal requirement, which does not depend on the doctor balancing interests.
This is a discretionary decision justified by weighing interests, so it is a public-interest disclosure.
Next of kin status gives no legal entitlement to information, so this is neither required by law nor a justified disclosure on its own.
A third party’s wish for information does not create a legal duty to disclose; consent would be needed.
questions.clue: The question asks for the disclosure that is required by law, not decided by the doctor.
questions.concept: Required by law vs public interest vs consent.

followUp.q: A patient with uncontrolled epilepsy keeps driving despite repeated advice to stop and refuses to tell the DVLA. After telling him what she plans to do, his doctor informs the DVLA. Which route best describes the disclosure?
options: Consent, because he was told beforehand
Required by law, because doctors must report every patient with epilepsy
Public interest, justified by the risk of serious harm to others, disclosing only the minimum necessary
Direct care, because the DVLA is part of the healthcare team
followUp.why: The doctor weighs the risk of serious harm to other road users against the patient's interest in confidentiality, so the justification is the public interest; she discloses only the relevant medical information to the DVLA and records her decision. Telling him first is good practice but is not consent, there is no legal duty on doctors to report every patient with epilepsy, and the DVLA does not provide his care. Check the current GMC guidance before applying it.

questions.q: A woman telephones a ward and says she is the daughter of an elderly patient who has capacity. She asks what the diagnosis is and says she is the next of kin. What is the best response?
options: Explain that you cannot share information without the patient’s permission and offer to ask the patient whether she may be updated
Give the diagnosis, because next of kin are entitled to information
Give the diagnosis if she can confirm the patient’s date of birth
Say nothing at all, and refuse to listen if she wishes to give information
questions.why: With a capacitous patient, ask what they are content to share and with whom. Next of kin status and identity details do not provide authority, but you can listen to the caller and then check the patient’s wishes. Refusing to listen is unnecessary.
optWhy: There is no automatic entitlement for next of kin when the patient has capacity.
Knowing identifying details does not give her permission; identity checks do not replace the patient’s consent.
Listening to information from relatives does not breach confidentiality; the problem is giving out information.
The patient has capacity, so her wishes decide who is told.
questions.clue: The patient has capacity and the caller relies on being next of kin.
questions.concept: Patient’s wishes govern disclosure to relatives.

followUp.q: A patient with capacity says she does not want her husband told about her diagnosis. He asks a nurse for an update. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell him, because he is her husband
Decline to give the information, explain that she cannot discuss patients without their permission, and listen to any concerns he raises
Tell him the diagnosis if he promises not to repeat it
Tell him, because she is likely to change her mind
followUp.why: The patient has capacity and has said no, so her decision is respected regardless of the relationship. A promise from the husband or a guess about her future wishes does not provide permission. The nurse can listen without disclosing.

questions.q: A capacitous patient receiving treatment from a surgical team says she does not want her GP told about her diagnosis. The GP is not otherwise involved in the current episode. What should the doctor do?
options: Stop treating the patient until she agrees
Inform the GP anyway because sharing for direct care never requires agreement
Inform the GP because doctors are bound by confidentiality, so the patient is not harmed
Explain the consequences of not sharing, and if she still objects, respect her decision unless an exception applies
questions.why: Direct-care sharing is the default but depends on the patient not objecting. The doctor explains what not sharing could mean and then respects her choice unless the law requires disclosure or it is justified in the public interest. The GP’s professional duty of confidence is not itself a justification, and treatment is not withdrawn.
optWhy: The GMC principle on direct care is expressed as sharing unless the patient has objected, so objection matters.
The GP’s own duty of confidence does not remove the need for a justified basis for the disclosure.
GMC guidance supports sharing for direct care unless the patient has objected.
Care should not be withdrawn because a patient objects to sharing; the doctor explains the implications and continues to care within what she has agreed.
questions.clue: She objects to sharing with her GP, who is not involved in this episode.
questions.concept: Respect for patient objection to sharing.

followUp.q: A capacitous patient asks you not to tell the physiotherapist about a recent mental health admission, because she finds it embarrassing. The physiotherapist does not need it to treat her knee. What is the best approach?
options: Respect her request and share only what the physiotherapist needs to treat her knee
Tell the physiotherapist, because every professional involved needs the full record
Tell the physiotherapist because she is part of the care team
Tell the physiotherapist but ask her to keep it confidential
followUp.why: Information shared for direct care should be relevant to the care being given, and she has objected. The admission is not needed for knee treatment, so there is no basis to share it. Being part of the care team does not mean access to everything, and asking the physiotherapist to keep it confidential does not justify an unnecessary disclosure.

questions.q: Explain the circumstances in which a doctor may disclose identifiable patient information without the patient’s consent.
markScheme: Where required by law (for example a court order); disclose only what the law requires
Where justified in the public interest: benefit to others outweighs harm to the patient and to trust in confidentiality
Disclose the minimum necessary to the appropriate person or body
Record the reasoning, seek advice where unsure, and tell the patient unless it is unsafe or impracticable
questions.modelAnswer: Identifiable information can be disclosed without consent in two main situations. First, where the law requires it, such as a court order or statutory duty, in which case the doctor discloses only what is required. Second, where disclosure is justified in the public interest, for example to protect others from serious harm. This requires weighing the harm of disclosure to the patient and to public trust in confidential care against the benefit of disclosure. The doctor should disclose only the minimum necessary to the appropriate person or body, record the decision and reasoning, and seek advice from a senior colleague, information governance lead or defence body if unsure. Where possible and safe, the patient should be told. Sharing information for direct care within the care team is also expected, unless the patient has objected.
questions.concept: Disclosure without consent needs a legal duty or a weighed public-interest justification.

questions.q: According to the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey 2023/4, what proportion of 16–64-year-olds in England had a common mental health condition?
questions.why: APMS 2023/4 found 22.6% of 16–64-year-olds in England had a common mental health condition, up from 18.9% in 2014 and 17.6% in 2007. The 26.2% figure applies to the most deprived fifth of areas, where prevalence was higher than in the least deprived fifth (16%).
optWhy: This is the 2014 figure for the same age group, so it reflects reading a different survey year.
This is the 2023/4 headline figure for this age group.
This is the 2007 figure for the same age group, so it also reflects the wrong survey year.
This is the figure for people in the most deprived fifth of areas, not the population as a whole.
questions.clue: The question asks for the 2023/4 overall figure for 16–64-year-olds.
questions.concept: APMS 2023/4 prevalence with year labels.

followUp.q: Which APMS 2023/4 finding best illustrates the link between social circumstances and mental health?
options: 22.6% of 16–64-year-olds had a common mental health condition
47.7% of people with symptoms reported receiving treatment
10.3% of 16–74-year-olds reported lifetime non-suicidal self-harm
26.2% of people in the most deprived fifth of areas had a common mental health condition, compared with 16% in the least deprived fifth
followUp.why: The comparison between most and least deprived areas shows a gradient. The overall 22.6% describes the population, the 47.7% describes treatment among those with symptoms, and the 10.3% describes self-harm; none compares social groups.

questions.q: A 24-year-old attends the emergency department after taking an overdose of her own tablets. A colleague suggests using a risk scale to classify her as low, medium or high risk and to discharge her if she scores low. What is the best response in line with NICE NG225?
options: Carry out a psychosocial assessment covering needs, risk factors and safety, and do not use a risk scale or risk category to decide who is offered treatment
Use the scale and discharge her if she scores low, because it predicts who will not repeat self-harm
Use the scale to predict suicide, but offer treatment to everyone regardless of the score
Assume the overdose was attention-seeking and offer no assessment
questions.why: NG225 recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.4 say not to use risk assessment tools or low/medium/high stratification to predict suicide or repetition or to decide who is offered treatment. A psychosocial assessment with a risk formulation is recommended instead, and a person’s needs, not a label, should drive their care.
optWhy: NG225 advises against using tools and stratification to determine who should be offered treatment.
NG225 says not to use risk tools to predict repetition of self-harm or future suicide, so a low score does not justify discharge without assessment.
Predicting suicide with a scale is itself what NG225 advises against, even if treatment is offered to everyone.
The reasons for self-harm vary, and NG225 expects an assessment of why it occurred and what the person needs; assuming attention-seeking is unfounded and unsafe.
questions.clue: A colleague suggests a low-risk score as the basis for discharge.
questions.concept: NG225: no risk-scale-based prediction or treatment allocation.

followUp.q: A junior doctor writes “high risk” in the notes after a patient’s self-harm and says this means she will be admitted, while “low risk” patients will not need follow-up. Which statement fits NG225?
options: The labels are valid if they are agreed by two doctors
High-risk labels may decide treatment, but low-risk labels may not
Risk labels should not decide who receives treatment; offer a psychosocial assessment and care based on needs and safety
Risk labels are required in the notes before any treatment is offered
followUp.why: NG225 advises against using stratification into low, medium or high risk to determine who is offered treatment, whoever agrees the label and whichever category is chosen. It also does not require a label before treatment, and instead recommends a risk formulation within a psychosocial assessment.

questions.q: During a mental state examination a man says, “My mood is fine.” You observe a flat expression, slowed movements and tears. Which term describes the emotional state you observe?
options: Affect
Mood
Thought form
Insight
questions.why: The observed emotional expression is affect, and a mismatch with reported mood is clinically useful. Thought form and insight are separate MSE domains.
optWhy: Mood is the patient’s own reported state, which in this case is “fine”; the flat, tearful presentation is the observed affect.
Thought form concerns the flow and coherence of thinking, not emotional expression.
Insight concerns whether he recognises that he has a problem, which the observation does not address.
Affect is the emotion observed by the examiner, whereas mood is the patient’s report.
questions.clue: He reports a fine mood but looks flat and tearful.
questions.concept: Mood is reported; affect is observed.

followUp.q: A woman describes feeling “terrible and hopeless” while smiling and laughing throughout. Which finding is this?
options: Normal mood and affect, because patients often smile when anxious
Mood and affect that do not match: her reported mood is low but her observed affect is cheerful
A disorder of thought form, because her speech is inconsistent
A hallucination, because she describes feelings not present on the surface
followUp.why: Describing hopelessness while appearing cheerful is a mismatch between mood (reported) and affect (observed), which should be explored. It is not a thought form disorder, since her speech flows coherently, nor a hallucination, which is a perception without a stimulus. It is not normal congruence.

questions.q: Describe the components of a mental state examination, giving one example of what you would look for in each.
markScheme: Appearance and behaviour (e.g. grooming, eye contact, psychomotor slowing)
Speech (rate, volume, fluency)
Mood (reported) and affect (observed)
Thought form and content (e.g. delusions, suicidal thoughts), and perception (hallucinations)
Cognition, insight and judgement; risk to self and others
questions.modelAnswer: The mental state examination is a structured description of the patient at interview. I would note appearance and behaviour, such as grooming, eye contact and psychomotor slowing or agitation; speech, such as rate, volume and fluency; and mood (what the patient says they feel) and affect (the emotion I observe, including whether it fits what they say). Under thought I would assess form (speed and coherence) and content, including delusions, obsessions and suicidal or violent thoughts, and note any beliefs that thoughts are inserted or broadcast. I would ask about perception, such as hallucinations. Cognition covers orientation, attention and memory. I would assess insight (whether they recognise a problem) and judgement. Finally I would record risk to self and others, including suicidal thoughts and self-harm.
questions.concept: The MSE gives a snapshot that complements the history.

questions.q: What is the maximum duration of detention under section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983?
options: 28 days, and it cannot be renewed
6 months, renewable
72 hours
14 days
questions.why: Section 2 is for assessment and lasts up to 28 days, with no renewal. The 72-hour period belongs to sections 4 and 5(2), the 14-day period is the tribunal application window (21 days once the 2025 Act change is in force), and six months renewable is section 3.
optWhy: This is the length of the doctor’s holding power under section 5(2) and of the emergency admission under section 4, not section 2.
Fourteen days is the current time limit for applying to the tribunal under section 2, not the length of detention.
Section 2 allows detention for up to 28 days beginning with admission.
This is the initial duration of section 3, the treatment section, not section 2.
questions.clue: The question asks for the duration of section 2.
questions.concept: Duration of section 2.

followUp.q: A patient admitted under section 2 still needs hospital treatment at day 25 and the diagnosis is now clear. What is the usual route?
options: Apply for detention under section 3 for treatment before section 2 expires
Renew section 2 for a further 28 days
Allow section 2 to lapse and use a nurse’s holding power instead
Use section 136 to continue the detention
followUp.why: Section 2 is not renewable, so continued compulsory treatment requires section 3 if the criteria are met. A nurse’s holding power is for voluntary inpatients and lasts only six hours, and section 136 is a police power to take someone to a place of safety, not a way to extend hospital detention.

questions.q: A voluntary patient on a surgical ward after an overdose says she is going home. A senior doctor assesses her and believes she has a mental disorder and is at serious risk. What is the most appropriate power to prevent her leaving while a formal assessment is arranged?
options: Section 5(4), because the nurses’ power is quicker
Section 3, which can be completed immediately by one doctor
Section 136, the police power to remove a person to a place of safety
Section 5(2): the doctor’s holding power for up to 72 hours
questions.why: The doctor’s holding power under section 5(2) applies to inpatients and lasts up to 72 hours. The nurses’ power under section 5(4) is for when a doctor is not immediately available. Section 136 is a police power, and section 3 requires two medical recommendations and an application, usually by an AMHP.
optWhy: Section 136 is exercised by police officers, not doctors, and is not the route for holding a voluntary inpatient while assessment is arranged.
Section 5(2) applies to voluntary inpatients and allows a doctor to hold them while assessment for detention is arranged.
Section 5(4) is the nurses’ power for use when a doctor is not immediately available. A doctor is already present, and 5(2) is the doctor’s power.
Section 3 needs two medical recommendations and an application, usually by an AMHP; it cannot be done instantly by one doctor.
questions.clue: Voluntary inpatient, doctor available, seeking to leave while assessment is arranged.
questions.concept: Holding powers for inpatients.

followUp.q: A voluntary psychiatric inpatient tries to leave and no doctor can attend for over an hour. A registered mental health nurse judges she is at risk. Which power is available to the nurse?
options: Section 5(2), the doctor’s power for 72 hours
Section 2, which a nurse can complete alone
Section 135, which allows the nurse to apply for a warrant
Section 5(4), the nurse’s holding power for up to 6 hours, with a doctor contacted immediately
followUp.why: Section 5(4) is the nurse’s holding power for voluntary inpatients when a doctor is not immediately available, and a doctor must be contacted at once. Section 5(2) is a doctor’s power, section 2 needs two doctors and an AMHP, and section 135 is a magistrate’s warrant for police entering premises.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia is detained under section 3. He has capacity and refuses his medication for the mental disorder. Which statement is correct?
options: Treatment for the mental disorder can be given under the Act without his consent, subject to its safeguards, even though he has capacity
Treatment must stop, because a person with capacity can always refuse treatment
Treatment can be given only after a best-interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act
Treatment can be given only if his relatives consent
questions.why: The MHA turns on mental disorder and risk rather than capacity, and authorises treatment for the mental disorder within safeguards such as the section 58 second-opinion certificate once medication continues beyond three months. Physical treatment unrelated to the disorder needs consent or MCA authority.
optWhy: The MHA does not depend on consent or on lack of capacity.
This applies to treatment outside the MHA. Under the Act, treatment for the mental disorder can be given without consent, with safeguards such as the second-opinion requirement.
Best interests applies when a person lacks capacity. The MHA authorises treatment of the mental disorder irrespective of capacity.
Relatives do not provide consent under the Act; the legal authority comes from the detention and its safeguards.
questions.clue: He is detained, has capacity and refuses medication for the mental disorder.
questions.concept: The MHA authorises treatment of mental disorder with or without consent.

followUp.q: The same detained man, who has capacity, refuses an operation to treat appendicitis. Which statement is correct?
options: The Act authorises any treatment for a detained patient
His relatives can consent on his behalf
The Act does not authorise this treatment; his capacitous refusal of treatment for a physical condition unrelated to his mental disorder must be respected
The Act authorises it if two doctors agree it is needed
followUp.why: The MHA authorises treatment of the mental disorder only. Appendicitis is unrelated, so a capacitous refusal stands. Relatives cannot consent for a capacitous adult, and agreement by two doctors does not expand the Act’s scope.

questions.q: Distinguish sections 2 and 3 of the Mental Health Act 1983, and explain how the Act relates to the Mental Capacity Act 2005.
markScheme: Section 2: assessment (or assessment then treatment), up to 28 days, not renewable
Section 3: treatment, up to 6 months initially and renewable
Both need two medical recommendations and an application, usually by an AMHP; section 2 grounds include own health or safety or protection of others
MHA depends on mental disorder and risk, not capacity; a capacitous person can be detained
MHA authorises treatment of the mental disorder only; physical illness needs consent or MCA authority
questions.modelAnswer: Section 2 allows admission for assessment, or assessment followed by treatment, for up to 28 days and cannot be renewed. Section 3 allows admission for treatment when the diagnosis and treatment needs are established; it lasts up to six months initially and can be renewed. Both need two medical recommendations and an application, usually by an approved mental health professional. Under section 2, the person must have a mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment, and ought to be detained in the interests of their own health or safety or for the protection of others. The Mental Health Act depends on mental disorder and risk, not capacity, so a person with capacity can be detained and treated for the mental disorder without consent, with safeguards. Lack of capacity alone does not justify detention under it. The Act covers treatment of the mental disorder; treatment of unrelated physical illness needs consent or authority under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 if the person lacks capacity.
questions.concept: The MHA and MCA address different questions.

questions.q: What does the Swiss cheese model of accident causation illustrate?
options: Harm is caused by a single careless individual, so discipline is the main remedy
Active failures last for years, whereas latent conditions are brief and visible
Adverse events are random and cannot be reduced by redesigning systems
Harm occurs when weaknesses in several layers of defence line up, so improving the system matters as well as individual performance
questions.why: In the model, each defence has holes, and an incident occurs when holes in several layers line up. Most incidents involve both active failures and latent conditions, so system improvements are more effective than blaming individuals.
optWhy: This is the person approach, which Reason argued is ill suited to healthcare because it ignores the system conditions behind errors.
This reverses the pattern: active failures are usually short-lived, whereas latent conditions can lie dormant for years.
The model implies the opposite: because latent conditions can be found and fixed in advance, the system can be made more resilient.
It pictures layers of defence with holes that can align, allowing a hazard to reach the patient.
questions.clue: The question asks what the Swiss cheese model illustrates.
questions.concept: Swiss cheese model: alignment of weaknesses.

followUp.q: A patient receives the wrong medicine because a similar-looking package, a busy ward and a skipped second check all coincided. Which interpretation best fits the Swiss cheese model?
options: The error was caused solely by the nurse who gave the medicine
Several weaknesses in different layers of defence lined up, so the response should look at the system as well as the individual
The error shows that checks are pointless
The error was unpreventable and random
followUp.why: Look-alike packaging, ward pressure and a missed check are separate weaknesses that aligned. Blaming only the nurse is the person approach, abandoning checks would remove a layer of defence, and the combination of known conditions shows the event was preventable rather than random.

questions.q: A hospital patient has an unplanned return to theatre after a complication, requiring a moderate increase in treatment, and the harm is significant but not permanent. Which statement about the statutory duty of candour is correct?
options: The duty requires only a written letter, with no need to speak to the patient
The provider must notify the patient as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, with a true account of what is known, an apology and details of further enquiries, followed by written notification
The duty applies only if the patient or relatives request an explanation
The duty arises only if the hospital admits that negligence caused the harm
questions.why: Moderate harm for a health service body includes harm needing a moderate increase in treatment, such as an unplanned return to surgery. The provider must notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, with a true account and apology, then follow up in writing. Fault is not a precondition and the patient does not have to ask.
optWhy: The duty is triggered by the notifiable safety incident and its level of harm, not by an admission of fault.
Regulation 20 requires notification in person, followed by written notification, so a letter alone does not meet it.
This is the regulation 20 process for a notifiable safety incident.
The provider must notify the relevant person once it is aware of the incident; the patient does not need to ask.
questions.clue: Unplanned return to theatre with moderate harm points to a notifiable safety incident.
questions.concept: Regulation 20 process and trigger.

followUp.q: Which element is part of the initial notification under regulation 20?
options: An apology, meaning an expression of sorrow or regret about the incident
A statement that the provider accepts legal liability
A promise of financial compensation
A confidentiality agreement signed by the patient
followUp.why: The regulation requires an apology, defined as an expression of sorrow or regret, together with a true account and further enquiry advice. It does not require acceptance of liability, promises of compensation or any confidentiality agreement.

questions.q: A nurse notices that a blood sample was labelled with the wrong patient’s details, but spots the error before it is sent to the laboratory. No patient is harmed. What is the best course of action?
options: Do nothing further, because no harm occurred
Correct the problem and report it as a near miss through the incident reporting system
Report it only if the patient later complains
Report it only if it fits the national list of never events
questions.why: LFPSE exists to record patient safety events whether or not harm occurs, because near misses reveal weak defences that may cause harm another day. Reporting is not limited to complaints or to the narrow category of never events.
optWhy: Near misses are learning opportunities and the system relies on them being reported.
LFPSE records events whether or not harm results, and near misses show weak defences.
Waiting for a complaint misses the chance to learn before harm occurs.
LFPSE records a wide range of events; a never event is a specific serious category and is not the threshold for reporting.
questions.clue: A labelling error is caught before it reaches the laboratory, with no harm.
questions.concept: Report near misses to learn from them.

followUp.q: A junior doctor realises she nearly prescribed a test for the wrong patient but caught it during her own check. What is the best action?
options: Say nothing, because she corrected it herself
Wait to see whether the error recurs before reporting
Report it only if she is worried about being criticised
Record the near miss on the incident reporting system and tell her supervisor so the system can be examined
followUp.why: A caught error still shows a weakness (for example similar patient names or an unclear ordering process). Reporting is how organisations find latent conditions. Staying silent or waiting for recurrence removes the opportunity to learn, and the decision to report should not depend on fear of criticism.

questions.q: Distinguish the statutory duty of candour from the professional duty of candour.
markScheme: Statutory duty: regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014; falls on registered providers; enforced by CQC
Triggered by a notifiable safety incident reaching a defined level of harm (for health service bodies including death, severe harm, moderate harm or prolonged psychological harm)
Requirements: notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, true account, apology, written follow-up, records
Professional duty: GMC and NMC joint guidance; applies to individual professionals whenever care causes or could cause harm or distress
Professional duty includes telling the patient, apologising, offering a remedy or support, explaining effects, and being open with colleagues and regulators
questions.modelAnswer: The statutory duty is in regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014. It falls on registered providers, that is organisations, and is enforced by the Care Quality Commission. It is triggered by a notifiable safety incident that reaches a defined level of harm, which for health service bodies includes death, severe harm, moderate harm and prolonged psychological harm. The provider must notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, giving a true account of the facts known, an apology and advice on further enquiries, then follow up in writing and keep records. The professional duty is set out in joint GMC and NMC guidance and rests on individual doctors and nurses. It applies whenever care causes, or could cause, harm or distress, so its threshold is lower. The professional must tell the patient, apologise, offer an appropriate remedy or support, and explain the short- and long-term effects, and be open and honest with colleagues, employers and regulators.
questions.concept: The two duties differ in who bears them and the threshold that triggers them.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a protected characteristic under section 4 of the Equality Act 2010?
options: Gender reassignment
Socio-economic status (social class or income)
Marriage and civil partnership
Pregnancy and maternity
questions.why: The nine characteristics are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Social class and income are not included, although they strongly influence health.
optWhy: The nine protected characteristics do not include social class or income.
This is a protected characteristic, though it is frequently forgotten; it applies to people who are married or in a civil partnership.
This is a protected characteristic and covers treatment because of pregnancy or having recently given birth.
This is a protected characteristic and covers people proposing to undergo, undergoing or having undergone a process of changing sex.
questions.clue: The question asks which one is not on the list of nine characteristics.
questions.concept: The list of protected characteristics.

followUp.q: A GP practice treats a patient badly because of her religion. Which statement is correct?
options: This cannot be discrimination because religion is not a protected characteristic
This is only discrimination if the patient has a disability
This could be direct discrimination because religion or belief is a protected characteristic
This is only discrimination if the practice has more than 250 staff
followUp.why: Religion or belief is a protected characteristic, and treating someone less favourably because of it can be direct discrimination under section 13. A disability is not required, and there is no staffing threshold for the prohibition on discrimination by service providers.

questions.q: A GP practice requires all patients to book appointments through an online form. A patient with a learning disability cannot use the form and is unable to book. What is the practice’s obligation?
options: An obligation only if the adjustment costs nothing
To make reasonable adjustments so that he can book, such as accepting bookings by phone or in person
No obligation, because the same rule applies to every patient
An obligation only if the patient first makes a written request for an adjustment
questions.why: Section 20 of the Equality Act 2010 requires service providers to take reasonable steps where a rule, practice, feature or lack of aid puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage. The duty is anticipatory, not dependent on a written request, and cost is a factor in reasonableness rather than a bar.
optWhy: Equal application does not remove the duty. A neutral rule can disadvantage disabled people, which engages indirect discrimination and the duty to make adjustments.
The duty is anticipatory, so providers should not wait for formal requests.
The duty is to take reasonable steps; cost is one factor in deciding reasonableness but does not mean only free steps count.
Section 20 requires service providers to take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage to disabled people.
questions.clue: A uniform online booking rule disadvantages a patient with a learning disability.
questions.concept: Reasonable adjustments are required for disabled people.

followUp.q: A hospital sends appointment details only as text messages. A deaf patient who cannot use a mobile phone misses her appointment. Which statement is correct?
options: The hospital has done nothing wrong because the rule is the same for everyone
The hospital should consider reasonable adjustments, such as written letters or email, so that she has equal access
The hospital must wait for her to complain before changing anything
The hospital is only required to act if she can prove she is disabled with a certificate
followUp.why: A uniform rule can disadvantage disabled people, which is why the duty to make adjustments exists. The duty is anticipatory, so waiting for a complaint is not enough. The Act does not require a certificate before adjustments are considered.

questions.q: A medical student on placement repeatedly hears a senior doctor use racist language about a nurse in front of colleagues. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Raise the concern promptly with a supervisor, personal tutor or the medical school’s named contact, using a factual account
Post an anonymised description on social media
Ignore it, because students should not get involved
Confront the doctor publicly on the ward round in front of patients
questions.why: GMP expects concerns about behaviour to be raised through workplace policy, with advice sought where appropriate. For a student, that means a supervisor, tutor or medical school contact, with a factual record. Ignoring the behaviour, confronting publicly or posting online each fail in different ways.
optWhy: Failing to act leaves the nurse and the culture unprotected; raising concerns is a professional expectation that starts in training.
Public confrontation is unlikely to help, may harm patients and colleagues, and bypasses the processes designed to handle concerns safely.
GMP expects concerns to be raised through workplace or school processes, keeping a factual record.
Public posts must be accurate and honest, can breach confidentiality and may harm trust; they are not an appropriate route for raising concerns.
questions.clue: Repeated racist language by a senior doctor towards a nurse.
questions.concept: Speaking up through appropriate channels.

followUp.q: A student sees a colleague falsify an attendance record. Which response is most consistent with Good medical practice?
options: Report it to a supervisor or the medical school, because honesty and integrity are central to professional trust
Say nothing, because it affects only the colleague
Copy the colleague’s approach to avoid being disadvantaged
Tell friends privately instead of the medical school
followUp.why: Honesty and integrity are core duties, and falsifying records damages public trust. Silence leaves the problem unaddressed, copying it repeats the dishonesty, and telling friends does not use the processes designed to address concerns.

questions.q: Explain the main forms of discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 and describe the duty to make reasonable adjustments.
markScheme: Nine protected characteristics (s4), e.g. age, disability, race, sex
Direct discrimination (s13): less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic
Indirect discrimination (s19): neutral rule that disadvantages a group and is not justified
Harassment (s26) and victimisation (s27) described correctly
Reasonable adjustments (s20): reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage for disabled people; anticipatory; example
questions.modelAnswer: The Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics (section 4): age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Direct discrimination (section 13) is less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic. Indirect discrimination (section 19) occurs when a rule or practice applied to everyone puts people with a characteristic at a disadvantage and cannot be justified. Harassment (section 26) is unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates dignity or creates a hostile environment, and victimisation (section 27) is subjecting someone to a detriment because they did a protected act, such as bringing a claim, giving evidence or complaining under the Act. Service providers, including health services, must also make reasonable adjustments for disabled people (section 20): where a rule, practice, physical feature or lack of an auxiliary aid puts a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage, they must take reasonable steps to avoid it. The duty is anticipatory. An example is accepting appointment bookings by phone as well as online for a patient with a learning disability.
questions.concept: The Act addresses both direct unfairness and neutral rules that disadvantage.

questions.q: What does the social gradient in health mean?
options: Health differences between groups are mostly explained by genetic differences
Health differences exist only between the north and the south of England
Only people in the poorest group have worse health than everyone else
Health tends to be better at each step up the social ladder, so everyone below the top has a greater risk of worse health than those above
questions.why: The Marmot Review describes health as following a social gradient: the lower one’s social and economic position, the poorer one’s health tends to be, across the whole population. It is not limited to the poorest, to a genetic effect or to a regional split.
optWhy: This describes a threshold effect and is the misconception the gradient rejects, because even moderately advantaged groups do worse than the most advantaged.
It describes a graded relationship across the whole population.
The gradient is explained mainly by social and economic conditions, not by genetics.
Regional differences exist, but the gradient also runs within every region and area.
questions.clue: The question asks for the meaning of the term social gradient.
questions.concept: The social gradient in health.

followUp.q: A study finds that people in the middle of the income distribution have worse health than those at the top, but better health than those at the bottom. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: A threshold effect, in which only poverty harms health
Regression to the mean
Proportionate universalism
The social gradient
followUp.why: Health getting progressively worse at each step down the scale is the social gradient. A threshold effect would show worse health only at the bottom. Regression to the mean is a statistical artefact unrelated to social position, and proportionate universalism is a policy approach to the gradient, not a pattern in the data.

questions.q: The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020) reported that life expectancy at birth for men in England rose by 0.9 years between 2010 and 2018, compared with 2.2 years in 2000 to 2008. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Improvements in life expectancy sped up after 2010
The slowdown was greatest in the least deprived areas
Improvements in life expectancy slowed markedly after 2010
Life expectancy fell for all groups after 2010
questions.why: Comparing the 0.9-year gain (2010 to 2018) with the 2.2-year gain (2000 to 2008) shows the pace of improvement fell. Male life expectancy still rose, the fall was for women in the most deprived tenth, and the slowdown was greatest in more deprived areas.
optWhy: The gain in 2010 to 2018 was much smaller than in 2000 to 2008.
Male life expectancy still rose slightly; the fall in the report was for women in the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods, not all groups.
A gain of 0.9 years is less than 2.2 years, so the pace slowed.
The report found the slowdown greatest in more deprived areas, not the least deprived.
questions.clue: Men gained 0.9 years from 2010 to 2018, compared with 2.2 years from 2000 to 2008.
questions.concept: Interpreting changes in life expectancy trends.

followUp.q: In 2016–18 life expectancy for women was 81.7 years in the North East and 84.5 in London. What is the gap, and what does it indicate?
options: 2.2 years, indicating no regional pattern
4.5 years, indicating that London women live much longer than all others
2.8 years, indicating a regional inequality in life expectancy
0.9 years, indicating that regional differences are small
followUp.why: 84.5 minus 81.7 is 2.8 years, the same gap as for men, which shows a regional inequality. The 2.2 and 0.9 figures are male gains in other comparisons, not this gap, and 4.5 does not follow from the numbers.

questions.q: A local health board has a limited budget for a new child health programme. Which plan best illustrates proportionate universalism?
options: Offer the programme to all families, with more visits and support in the areas with the greatest disadvantage
Offer the programme only to families in the most deprived tenth of areas
Offer the identical programme to every family in the same amount
Distribute leaflets advising parents on healthy behaviour
questions.why: Proportionate universalism combines universal provision with scale and intensity proportionate to disadvantage. Targeting only the most deprived misses the gradient, identical provision ignores differing needs, and leaflets rely on individual behaviour change.
optWhy: This is targeting; it would miss the gradient, since families just above the cut-off also have worse outcomes than the best-off.
This is pure universalism; it may widen inequalities because those with greater need receive no extra support.
This is an individual-behaviour approach: it leaves unchanged the income, housing and work conditions that shape behaviour, and gives no extra support where disadvantage is greatest.
It combines universal reach with greater intensity where need is greatest.
questions.clue: The plan must reach everyone but with greater effort where disadvantage is greater.
questions.concept: Proportionate universalism in practice.

followUp.q: A GP practice offers all patients with diabetes a review, and adds home visits and evening clinics for patients who have missed several reviews because of work or caring duties. Which approach is this?
options: Pure targeting, because only some patients get a review
Proportionate universalism, because it serves everyone with extra effort for those facing the greatest barriers
Identical universal provision, because everyone gets the same service
Victim blaming, because it focuses on patients who miss reviews
followUp.why: Everyone is offered a review, and additional support goes to those facing barriers, which is the definition of proportionate universalism. It is not pure targeting since all patients are served, and not identical provision since intensity varies. Removing barriers is the opposite of blaming patients.

questions.q: Describe the social gradient in health and explain proportionate universalism. State three of the six policy objectives of the 2010 Marmot Review.
markScheme: Social gradient: health improves with each step up the social scale across the whole population; not just the poorest
Possible examples: seven years’ earlier death in the poorest neighbourhoods (2010 review)
Proportionate universalism: universal action with scale and intensity proportionate to disadvantage
Three correct objectives (e.g. best start in life; fair employment and good work; healthy standard of living; maximise capabilities; healthy and sustainable places; strengthen ill health prevention)
Reason: targeting only the most deprived misses the gradient
questions.modelAnswer: The social gradient means that health tends to improve at each step up the social and economic scale, so that everyone below the top has a greater risk of worse health than those above; it is not confined to the poorest. The 2010 Marmot Review reported, for example, that people in the poorest neighbourhoods die on average seven years earlier than those in the richest. Proportionate universalism is the principle of universal action to reduce the gradient, with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. Targeting only the most deprived would miss the gradient, whereas uniform provision would leave greater need unmet.
