Three of the six objectives are to give every child the best start in life, to create fair employment and good work for all, and to ensure a healthy standard of living for all. The others are to enable all to maximise their capabilities and control their lives, to create healthy and sustainable places and communities, and to strengthen ill health prevention.
questions.concept: The gradient affects everyone, and the response must be proportionate.

questions.q: Mrs Dale, aged 82, is on a medical ward with pneumonia and delirium. She has pulled out her cannula twice and says she wants to go home because staff are “keeping her here to steal her house”. She can repeat that she has a chest infection. Her daughter says, “I am her next of kin, so I will sign the consent form.” Discuss the legal and ethical approach to her treatment, with reference to the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and the principles of valid consent.
markScheme: Presume capacity (s1); capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; take all practicable steps to help her decide
Two-stage assessment: impairment or disturbance of mind or brain (delirium) and the s3 functional test; identify which ability fails (using or weighing)
Unwise decision alone is not incapacity; retention, understanding and communication may be intact; balance of probabilities and documentation
Daughter cannot consent as next of kin unless she holds a relevant lasting power of attorney or deputyship; she is consulted under s4
Best-interests decision (s4): regaining capacity, past and present wishes, beliefs and values, consultation, least restrictive option (s1(6)); s5 protection when acting
Treat the cause of delirium and reassess capacity; consider whether treatment can wait if capacity is likely to return
Valid consent principles: capacity, information, voluntariness; capacitous refusal must be respected; Montgomery dialogue once capacity returns
Communication and professionalism: calm, explanation, family involvement, record keeping, senior help
questions.modelAnswer: Mrs Dale’s care raises the questions of whether she can decide for herself, and, if she cannot, how a decision is made for her. Under section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) capacity is presumed, so the team must assess it for the specific decision about antibiotics and staying in hospital, at the time, after taking all practicable steps to help her decide. Those steps include explaining in simple language, making sure she has any hearing aid or glasses she uses, choosing a calm time and treating reversible causes of confusion. The assessment has two stages. First, is there an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain? Delirium from infection qualifies. Second, because of that, can she understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, and communicate a decision (section 3)? She can repeat that she has a chest infection, so understanding and communication may be intact, but she believes the staff are plotting to take her house and so cannot weigh the information. If, on the balance of probabilities, she cannot use or weigh the information, she lacks capacity for this decision. The refusal alone would not show this, since an unwise decision does not show incapacity (section 1). Her daughter cannot consent as next of kin: an adult’s relatives are consulted, but they have no general power to consent unless they hold a valid lasting power of attorney or deputyship covering the decision. The clinician makes a best-interests decision under section 4, considering whether she is likely to regain capacity (in which case the decision might wait if safe), her past and present wishes and values, the views of her daughter and others who know her, and the least restrictive option. Section 5 protects those who act reasonably in her best interests, but not against negligence. In practice the team treats the infection and its delirium, reassesses her capacity regularly, records the assessment and reasoning, and involves senior help if there is disagreement. Once she regains capacity, she is entitled to a proper discussion of risks and alternatives under Montgomery, and her decision then stands even if it appears unwise.
questions.concept: Applying the MCA to a patient with delirium, and who can consent.

questions.q: Discuss how social determinants contribute to mental health problems in England, using the findings of the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey 2023/4 and the Marmot reviews. What can doctors and health services do in response?
markScheme: Definition of social determinants and Dahlgren–Whitehead model; social gradient
APMS 2023/4 data with year labels: 22.6% (16–64) vs 18.9% (2014) and 17.6% (2007); 26.2% vs 16% by deprivation; women vs men; limiting physical condition 32.9% vs 12.6%
Pathways: material, psychosocial, behavioural, access, life course; reverse causation (illness affects income, work)
Marmot 2010: six objectives and proportionate universalism; 2020 update: life expectancy slowdown, widening inequalities
Limits of survey evidence: association not causation; reasons for trends debated
Clinical responses: ask, adapt (health literacy), reduce barriers, refer and signpost, advocate
System responses: proportionate universalism, collaboration with local government and voluntary sector, addressing early years and employment
Professional dimension: fairness, equality duties, avoiding blaming patients
questions.modelAnswer: Social determinants are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age and the wider forces that shape them. The Dahlgren–Whitehead model shows individual factors nested within lifestyle, community and environment, and broad socio-economic conditions. The Marmot reviews describe a social gradient: health worsens at each step down the social scale. The 2023/4 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey for England shows how this applies to mental health. It found 22.6% of 16–64-year-olds had a common mental health condition, compared with 18.9% in 2014 and 17.6% in 2007. Prevalence was 26.2% in the most deprived fifth of areas and 16% in the least deprived fifth, about 1.6 times higher, and 32.9% of people with a limiting physical health condition had a condition compared with 12.6% of those without. Several pathways plausibly link circumstances and mental health: material hardship and insecurity, chronic stress and low control, discrimination, isolation, and unequal access to help. Causation also runs the other way, since mental illness can reduce employment and income. The survey shows associations and cannot explain the rise over time, for which several explanations, including greater willingness to report, are debated. The Marmot Review (2010) proposed six objectives, starting with the best start in life for every child, and proposed proportionate universalism. The 2020 update found that life expectancy gains had slowed after 2010 (0.9 years for men and 0.6 for women between 2010 and 2018, compared with 2.2 and 1.5 in 2000 to 2008), that female life expectancy fell in the most deprived tenth of neighbourhoods and that inequalities had widened. Doctors can respond by asking about circumstances, adapting communication to health literacy, reducing barriers to access, referring to welfare, housing and employment support, and advocating for patients, while treating mental illness itself and avoiding blaming individuals. Services and local government can apply proportionate universalism, directing more intensive support to more disadvantaged areas, and work across sectors on early years, employment and housing. Good medical practice and equality law require fair treatment and reasonable adjustments.
questions.concept: Social determinants shape mental health through several linked pathways.

cases.title: Pulling out the cannula: capacity and consent

steps.text: Mrs Dale, 82, was admitted two days ago with pneumonia. She was previously independent, with a mild memory complaint. This morning the nurse tells you she has pulled out her intravenous cannula twice, says she wants to go home, and tells staff, “You are keeping me here to steal my house.” Her daughter says that, as next of kin, she will sign whatever is needed.

ask.q: What is the correct first step in deciding about her treatment?
options: Assess her capacity for this specific decision, presuming capacity and first taking practicable steps to help her decide
Record that she lacks capacity because she is 82 and has memory problems
Ask her daughter to consent as next of kin
Restrain her and give the treatment immediately without further assessment
ask.why: The MCA presumes capacity and requires decision-specific assessment after practicable steps to help. Age and a memory complaint do not establish incapacity, a next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless holding a relevant legal authority, and restraint without assessment and a best-interests decision is not justified.

steps.text: You speak to her in a quiet room with her hearing aid in. She can say she has a “chest infection” and repeats that the antibiotics are “to make me better”. But she then says the doctors have a plan to take her home from her and that the drip is part of it. A delirium screen is positive and her temperature is raised.

ask.q: How should her capacity be judged?
options: She lacks capacity for this decision at present: there is a disturbance of brain function (delirium) and she cannot use or weigh the information because of her belief
She has capacity, because she can repeat the information and state her choice
She lacks capacity, because refusing antibiotics is an unwise decision
She lacks capacity for all decisions, because delirium has been diagnosed
ask.why: Delirium satisfies the diagnostic stage, and her belief prevents her using or weighing the information, which satisfies the functional stage even though she can repeat facts. An unwise decision alone would not show incapacity, and capacity is decision-specific and time-specific rather than all-or-nothing.

steps.text: Having decided she lacks capacity for this decision at this time, the team must decide how to proceed. Her daughter holds no lasting power of attorney. Mrs Dale has previously told her daughter that she hates hospitals but “would want to be well enough to stay in my own home”.

options: Make a best-interests decision under section 4: consider that she may regain capacity, her past and present wishes and values, consult her daughter, choose the least restrictive option, and record the reasons
Let the daughter sign the form, since she is next of kin
Respect the refusal and discharge her, because patients can always refuse treatment
Proceed with treatment without recording anything, because she cannot object
ask.why: The MCA requires a best-interests decision that takes account of her wishes and values, the chance she regains capacity and the views of those close to her, using the least restrictive option and recording the reasoning. A next of kin without legal authority cannot consent, a refusal made without capacity does not carry the same weight, and records are essential.

steps.text: The team treats the pneumonia using the least restrictive approach and works to settle her: reorientation, glasses and hearing aid, her daughter visiting, and treating her delirium. After three days her delirium has settled. Her capacity is reassessed and she understands and weighs the information, and she decides to continue treatment and to go home with support when well enough.

debrief: Capacity is presumed, decision-specific and time-specific: assess it for this decision and reassess as the delirium changes.
A diagnosis, age or an unwise decision does not by itself show lack of capacity; apply the section 3 test.
Next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a lasting power of attorney or deputyship; relatives are consulted in a best-interests decision.
Best interests (section 4) centres the person’s wishes, values and chance of regaining capacity, using the least restrictive option.
Once capacity returns, the patient’s own informed decision stands.

cases.title: The follow-up that was never booked: an incident and candour

steps.text: You are a medical student on a GP placement. While reviewing records with your supervisor, you notice that Mr Hassan, 63, had a chest X-ray in the emergency department five weeks ago. The report suggested a follow-up CT scan if symptoms continued, but nothing in the record shows that anyone acted on the recommendation. He has just booked an appointment because of a persistent cough.

options: Tell your supervisor straight away, so that the patient’s care can be reviewed
Telephone Mr Hassan yourself to explain what has happened
Say nothing, because you are only a student
Add a note to the earlier record so it looks as though the recommendation was acted on
ask.why: Patient safety comes first, and the clinical team is responsible for acting and for speaking to the patient. A student should tell their supervisor promptly. Contacting the patient alone is outside your role, staying silent leaves risk unaddressed, and altering records is dishonest.

steps.text: Your supervisor confirms that the CT was never booked because the report was filed without anyone being named as responsible. Mr Hassan is arranged for an urgent scan and a specialist referral. His cough and a recent weight loss mean the delay might matter.

ask.q: What does the duty of candour require of the clinicians now?
options: Tell Mr Hassan openly what happened, apologise, explain the likely short- and long-term effects, and offer support to put things right
Wait until the investigation has finished before telling him anything
Tell him only if he asks directly
Tell his relatives first so that they can decide how much he should know
ask.why: The professional duty of candour applies where care causes, or could cause, harm or distress: tell the person, apologise, offer a remedy or support, and explain the effects. Waiting, waiting for questions, or telling relatives first fails the duty. The organisation will also consider whether the statutory duty is triggered.

steps.text: The practice records the event in the national reporting system and starts a review. A colleague says, “We should find out who filed that report and make sure it does not happen again.”

ask.q: Which approach best fits a system-based, learning-focused response (such as PSIRF)?
options: Examine how results and recommendations are routed, who owns follow-up, and which barriers failed, with the patient involved and staff supported
Identify and discipline the person who filed the report as the main response
No review is needed once the apology has been given
Keep the event within the practice and avoid recording it nationally
ask.why: A system approach asks how and why defences failed, such as the lack of a named owner for results, and uses compassionate engagement and proportionate learning. Blaming the last person ignores latent conditions, an apology does not replace learning, and events should be recorded so that learning can be shared.

steps.text: The review finds no process for tracking recommended follow-up from reports. The practice introduces a rule that each report with an action is assigned to a named clinician, with a prompt if it is not acknowledged within a set time. Mr Hassan is told the findings. The provider considers whether the statutory duty applies according to the level of harm, and ensures that any written notification required is sent.

debrief: Tell your supervisor promptly if you see an error or near miss; do not hide it, alter records or explain it to the patient yourself.
The professional duty of candour applies whenever care causes or could cause harm or distress: tell, apologise, offer remedy or support, and explain.
The statutory duty (regulation 20) falls on the provider and depends on the level of harm; it requires in-person notification, an apology and written follow-up.
Look for latent conditions, such as no named owner for results, rather than blaming the last person.
Record events in the national system whether or not they cause harm so that the NHS can learn.

osce.title: Breaking bad news (SPIKES)
steps: Wash your hands, introduce yourself with your name and role, confirm the patient’s identity and explain that you would like to talk about the results; ask permission to proceed
Prepare beforehand: know the facts and the plan, find a private room, silence your phone, have tissues available, and ask whether the patient wants someone with them
Setting up: sit down at the patient’s level with no barrier between you, and keep appropriate eye contact
Perception: ask what the patient understands so far about their condition and what they have been told or suspect
Invitation: ask how much they would like to know and whether they would like the full results today
Give a warning shot, for example “I’m afraid the news is serious”, before giving the result
Knowledge: give the headline in plain, jargon-free language in short chunks, with no euphemisms, and pause after each chunk
Allow silence and watch the patient’s response; do not rush to fill the gap
Emotions: acknowledge the emotion you see with an empathic statement and offer support or tissues, giving time before continuing
Check understanding and explore their immediate ideas and concerns; answer questions honestly, admit uncertainty and avoid false reassurance
Strategy: outline the next steps in a few clear stages and who will do them; do not push for decisions at this meeting
Summarise the key points, invite further questions and ask how they are feeling
Safety-net and support: give a named contact such as a specialist nurse, offer written information and arrange follow-up; ask about support at home and whether they are safe to travel
Document the conversation, inform the relevant team and, if appropriate, the GP; thank the patient and wash your hands
tips: Use the patient’s name and avoid medical jargon; say the key word (for example “cancer”) clearly if that is the news.
Silence is a skill; resist the urge to fill it after a reaction.
Do not guess at prognosis or time frames, or promise outcomes you cannot guarantee; say honestly what is and is not yet known.
If the patient does not want to hear details now, respect this and offer another time.
SPIKES is a framework and not a script; follow the patient’s lead.
